label: refute:correctness:Physical-world tools are gated identical

result.concern: Verification of the whole: test-suite shape, integration/e2e tests, trial harness, observer kit, benchmark unit, tracing/observability, findings process, and the Verification subsystem's role
result.summary_of_what_is_actually_there: Two test trees coexist: tests/simorgh/ (405 files, 5,515 test functions, 2,553 async) for the v2 system, and tests/test_*.py (41 files, 11,574 lines, 887 test functions) which import only the dead v1 tree src/ (16,441 lines that nothing under simorgh/ imports; src last touched 2026-09-09, its tests 2026-09-06). There is no pytest.ini/pyproject/CI; the only configuration is the root conftest.py, which strips every SIMORGH_* variable and every model key from the session and forces SIMORGH_COGNITION_PROVIDER_ORDER=floor so booted Kernels answer offline (conftest.py:30-71), and registers a single `live` marker used by 6 files, all under tests/simorgh/execution. The bootloader simloader.py gates a checkout with a curated CORE_TESTS list (simloader.py:530-542, `-m "not live"`, six execution domains ignored) and reads pytest's own summary line rather than its exit code, refusing empty, skipped or shrunken runs (simloader.py:641-700); the last gate ran 3,348 tests in 45s (.simorgh_loader/unit_baseline-core.json). The trial suite (tools/trial_suite.py) boots a real Kernel in a copy-on-write repo clone, files one human task per trial, waits for a terminal status and judges the system's behaviour (commit made or not, tree clean, tool faults that are ours, ledger verify verdicts), but it only runs under `bless --full`, calls a paid model, takes ~25 minutes serially and depends on Together being up. The last full run (2026-09-18 14:00) was 3/7 clean and the creator then blessed four commits unit-only (decisions.jsonl). Integration tests are genuine: 43 files construct a real Kernel (33 in tests/simorgh/integration), test_kernel_boots_all_sixteen_subsystems boots all 17 real services, test_cli_end_to_end drives 17 lines through the real Interface `_handle_line`, and two architecture tests enforce import boundaries by AST and that a config section actually reaches its service. Nothing in tests/simorgh spawns `python -m simorgh` as a process; the only process-boundary e2e is the v1 tests/test_e2e_cli.py. The Verification subsystem registers 11 mechanical checks (simorgh/verification/checks/__init__.py:13-25) but the orchestration path hands it a subject of description/result/kind/steps/complete_log/subject/written_paths/base_ref/repo_root with wire kind always "task" (orchestration/session.py:1741, 1885-1890), so five checks whose `applies()` needs `candidate`/`code`/`original` or kind=="skill" never run, and the live ledger confirms it: over 349 sampled verify streams only six check names ever appear, verdicts split 220 fail / 109 pass / 21 insufficient_evidence, and full_suite_ran failed 56 of 62 times. Tracing writes one `trace:<id>` stream per root message (bus/trace.py:101) with a hand-maintained exclusion list (bus/config.py:60-64); the live ledger holds 88,356 trace streams from two days, 76% of a 400-file sample containing exactly one event, chat turns yield 2-event islands (think + reply) and voice turns 1-event islands, while only task sessions produce a chain. The benchmark unit (simorgh/benchmark) scores GAIA/BFCL/SWE-bench model capability; there is no latency or regression benchmark of the chat/voice path (only tools/bench_recall.py for memory retrieval and voice/bench.py for one STT sample). Findings are recorded in docs/findings (5 dated files since 2026-09-15), alongside a 5,254-line EVOLUTION.md, ~40 memory notes and observer findings JSONL under ~/.cache.
strengths: The loader never runs the code it judges and does not trust its exit byte: simloader.py:641-700 parses pytest's own summary line, rejects 'no tests ran', rejects a suite that shrank >10% against the last green baseline, and each of those rules is annotated with the live attack it closed (deleted tests, conftest exit-status override, blanket skip marker). This is a correct A/B-image design for a self-editing program.

The root conftest.py (lines 30-71) isolates the whole session from the operator's environment and model keys and forces the offline floor provider; the docstring records the incident (84 fake memories written into the live ledger by tests) that motivated it. Deterministic, unbilled unit runs are a precondition for everything else and they got it right.

Architecture-level tests exist and are mechanical: tests/simorgh/test_module_boundaries.py enforces the blueprint's import rules by AST and self-tests the checker against a temp tree; tests/simorgh/test_every_subsystem_reads_its_config.py asserts a toml value arrives in the service rather than that a config attribute exists; tests/simorgh/integration/test_kernel_boots_all_sixteen_subsystems.py boots all 17 real services through the real registry.

tests/simorgh/integration/test_cli_end_to_end.py (17 cases) starts where a human starts (a typed line through the real booted Interface) and asserts on what Planning and Orchestration did with it; its docstring names the three seam bugs unit tests structurally cannot see. 33 of the 42 integration files boot a real Kernel; 103 of the last 130 commits touch code and tests together.

tools/trial_suite.py judges the system, not the model: a task ending blocked/failed, a dirty tree, an unparseable file, a tool fault in the _OUR_FAULT list; commits are counted with `git rev-list --count` after a substring judge was fooled (trial_suite.py:171-186); a safety block is accepted only when the ledger's own verify.result shows `full_suite_ran` fired (trial_suite.py:255-285). The trial suite is the one instrument that found the 2026-09-07 blockers, and the project documents that honestly (simloader.py:26-29).

The mechanical checks that do run are each born from one live incident and scoped narrowly with the cost stated: did_anything (checks/didanything.py:1-30), trailing_narration (checks/trailing_narration.py:1-20), full_suite_ran with baseline attribution so a pre-existing red suite is not blamed on the change (checks/fullsuiteran.py:31-60).

Trace volume is controlled by excluding whole message types and by 2-day retention rather than fractional sampling, with the reasoning written down (bus/config.py:39-58); retention demonstrably works today (oldest trace stream Sep 16 13:57, newest Sep 18 17:14, 0 streams older than 2 days).

The observer kit (tools/observer_kit.py) solves real measured costs -- copy-on-write repo clones, collision-free workspaces, JSONL findings clustered by tools/aggregate_findings.py -- and docs/observer-testing.md states plainly what did and did not get faster. For a one-person project whose workforce is parallel AI agents, this is proportionate infrastructure.

findings.title: The only check that catches real blockers is optional and is being skipped
findings.claim: The loader's own docstring says a known-good tag is earned by 'the unit suite plus the scored trial suite', but run_gate only runs trials under --full, and the decision log shows the creator blessing four commits unit-only right after a full bless was refused for trial failures.
evidence: simloader.py:26-29: 'The gate that earns one is the unit suite plus the scored trial suite -- because this week 2,600 passing tests sat on top of a system that could not write a file, and the trial suite is the check that would have caught it.'
simloader.py:609-611: `if not full: return True, f"unit suite green ({unit_why})"` -- trials never run on `run`, only on `bless --full`.

.simorgh_loader/decisions.jsonl tail: `{"ts": 1789765232, "kind": "bless_refused", "commit": "e317076", "why": "trial suite had failures"}` followed 187s later by `{"ts": 1789765419, "kind": "blessed", "commit": "e317076", "tag": "sim-good-0020", "why": "unit suite green (3348 tests ran, none failed)"}`; sim-good-0021, 0022, 0023 all 'unit suite green'.
.simorgh_loader/last_green.json: `{"commit": "93764b7...", "full": false, "all_tests": false}`.

.simorgh_loader/last_trials.txt: `3/7 clean`; FAIL edit-an-existing-file (blocked), research-a-question (blocked), already-done, continues-across-attempts; trial wall times 299+181+236+45+374+327+71 = 1533s; Together 503s mid-run ('cognition.provider_failed provider=together ... Service unavailable').
findings.why_it_matters: The bootloader's promise is that a sim-good tag means independently verified; today it means 'the unit suite that has never caught a real blocker was green'. Sim's self-patches and the creator's own edits both roll forward on that tag. The trial suite is 25 minutes, costs money and fails on third-party outages, so the human rationally skips it, and the design silently degrades to exactly the gate the docstring says is insufficient.
findings.recommendation: Make a cheap trial subset part of `bless` by default: two trials (create-a-file and breaks-the-suite, ~6 min) with autonomy off and a `--unit-only` flag that must be typed to skip them. Record the trial verdict (n/7 clean) in the tag's decision note and refuse to tag when it is worse than the previous tag's. Treat a provider 503 as 'not judged' rather than FAIL so an outage cannot block a bless, and cache the last trial verdict per source hash the way gate_reused already caches the unit result.

findings.title: Five of eleven mechanical checks can never run on the real path, and the rigor table is inert
findings.claim: Orchestration's verify subject never carries candidate/code/original and always sends wire kind 'task', so denylist_immunity, docstring, invariants, isolated_suite and sandbox_smoke are dead for every human or trial task, and select_rigor resolves every task to STANDARD regardless of the configured patch=FULL / research=LIGHT / skill=FULL table.
evidence: simorgh/orchestration/session.py:1885-1890 subject keys: `"description", "result", "kind", "steps", "complete_log", "subject", "written_paths", "base_ref", "repo_root"`; grep for '"candidate"|"code":|"original"|"path":' in session.py returns only an unrelated git_discard arg at line 864.
simorgh/orchestration/session.py:1741: `"kind": "task", "subject_ref": subject_ref` -- session.kind (patch/skill/research) is not the wire kind.

checks/invariants.py:28-31, checks/docstring.py:45-48, checks/denylist_immunity.py:21-22, checks/isolated_suite.py:18-19 all require `req.subject.get("candidate") or req.subject.get("code")`; checks/sandbox_smoke.py:28 `return req.kind == "skill"`.

verification/rigor.py:22-25 with config.py:14-26: `rigor_by_kind.get("task", Rigor.STANDARD)` -- 'task' is not in the table; service.py:162 `reversibility=subject.get("reversibility", "reversible")` -- never sent, so STANDARD both ways; service.py:172-174 FULL only adds isolated_suite, which cannot apply.

Live ledger probe over 349 verify streams: only ('did_anything','full_suite_ran','js_syntax','render','syntax','trailing_narration') ever appear as mechanical results; verdicts `fail 220 / pass 109 / insufficient_evidence 21`.
checks/fullsuiteran.py:5-13 already documents that IsolatedSuiteCheck never fires for this reason; the four siblings with the same applies() condition were not noticed.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the verification-side consequence of the already-known dead Learning pipeline, and it is materially larger than 'one tool is not registered': the subsystem's design (11 checks, cheapest-first, reversibility-weighted rigor) is what the docs and the tests describe, but the running system is 6 checks at one rigor. Research tasks pay a model call for a checklist they were configured to skip; skills never get the sandbox smoke; and tests/simorgh/verification/test_invariants.py and test_docstring.py assert the shape of code the system never executes -- the exact failure mode the project's own notes describe.
findings.recommendation: Pick one of two honest states. Either (a) make the checks reachable: have _put_verify_subject send session.kind as the wire kind and, for each written path, read the worktree file into subject['candidates'][path] (the worktree is already at session.worktree), and rewrite the four content checks to iterate written paths; or (b) delete the five dead checks, the rigor table and their tests, leaving the six that run. Add one integration assertion that every check in ALL_CHECKS has fired at least once against the subject shape orchestration actually sends.

findings.title: full_suite_ran fails 90% of the time because 'the whole suite' is the wrong oracle inside a task
findings.claim: The load-bearing gate for self-patching demands a run of `tests` (all 6,000 tests, ~2 minutes, including v1 and feature suites that are environment-sensitive) inside every patch task, and it fails 56 of the 62 times it has run in the live ledger.
evidence: Live ledger probe: `('full_suite_ran', 'failed') 56`, `('full_suite_ran', 'passed') 6`.

.simorgh_loader/last_trials.txt line 8: `run_tests([ran target='tests'] [failed 4: tests/simorgh/execution/media/test_cast.py:...  ✗ 1.8m` inside the create-a-file trial; the same file on the host: `python3 -m pytest -q tests/simorgh/execution/media/test_cast.py` -> `32 passed, 2 warnings in 32.41s`, i.e. the lab's suite was red for reasons unrelated to the change.
last_trials.txt lines 150-158: `verification fail: mechanical check failed -- run_tests was called on a narrower target` three times, then `blocked in 70s -- verification failed after max revisions`.
checks/fullsuiteran.py:31-60 describes the 'objection that could not be answered' and adds baseline attribution, which still needs a second full run to answer it.
simloader.py:530-554 already defines the curated 45-second CORE selection with `-m "not live"`; the in-task check does not use it.
findings.why_it_matters: Verification's job is to give a patch a fast, attributable yes/no. A two-minute oracle that is red on this machine for unrelated reasons, running inside a step budget, converts the check into a revision loop that ends in 'blocked' -- the last_trials output shows exactly that. The creator then sees tasks blocked and blesses without trials (finding 1). The check is right; the suite it points at is the loader's `--all-tests` set, not the loader's gate.
findings.recommendation: Define the suite once: expose simloader.gate_selection() (or a tests/core.txt it reads) and have run_tests' 'whole suite' mean that CORE selection, so the in-task oracle is the same 45-second set the loader blesses on. Persist the last green gate's failure set per machine and have _baseline consult it before re-running anything. Mark the feature suites (media, home, voice engines) `live` or keep them out of CORE so they cannot make the oracle red.

findings.title: Tracing produces 46k one-event streams a day and no end-to-end trace for a chat or voice turn
findings.claim: The per-root-message trace design with a hand-maintained exclusion list yields mostly single-event streams from topics that were never excluded, while the daily path (a typed or spoken turn) leaves only a two-event think/reply island, so `simorgh trace <id>` cannot reconstruct a bad turn.
evidence: Measured on ~/.simorgh/ledger/streams: `streams total: 118215  trace: 88356  non-trace: 29859`, `trace in last 24h: 46264`; 400-file sample: 228 streams with 1 line, 54 with 2, 16 with 3, 2 with 14.

One-event roots by type (400 sample): world.camera.event 52, ui.notice 51, ui.hook.received 44, persona.state.changed 42, voice.listening 31, tool.registered 21, voice.transcript 18 -- none of these are in the exclusion list at bus/config.py:60-64 (`system.tick.*`, `system.metrics`, `system.health`, `cognition.provider.status`, `_inbox.#`).
3000-file sample: traces containing cognition.think by length `[(2, 69), (12, 1), (14, 4), (27, 1), (271, 1)]`; traces rooted at voice.transcript `[(1, 130)]` -- every voice turn is an orphan.
session.py:1291 `trace_id=session.task_id` on the think request; the inbound line/transcript and the outbound reply (private inbox, `_inbox.#` sampled to 0.0) never share it.
kernel/cli.py:37 and 242-256 implement `simorgh trace <id>`; grep 'trace' in interface/tui.py returns only traceback-formatting lines (390-400), so no turn ever shows a human its trace id.
kernel/metrics.py:17-27 notes that mining trace streams is already 'a dead end in practice' and adds a separate metrics:history stream.
findings.why_it_matters: The blueprint's tracing exists to answer 'what happened on that turn'; on this system it answers it only for task sessions, which are the minority path, while costing ~46k files a day of write and retention work on a JSONL ledger that is already 1.4 GB. For a one-laptop, one-family system the interesting unit is the turn, not the message.
findings.recommendation: Invert the policy: trace only messages that carry a partition_key or task_id (an allow-list of causal topics), which removes the periodic roots without maintaining a denylist. Assign one turn id at the Interface line / voice transcript, pass it as trace_id through session, think, verify and voice.speak, and add a TUI `trace` (or `last`) command that prints the last turn's id and its chain. Measure the file count a day later.

findings.title: 11.5k lines of tests and a verification invariant guard the dead v1 tree
findings.claim: The 41 top-level tests/test_*.py files (887 tests) import only src/, which nothing under simorgh/ imports, yet they remain in `--all-tests`, in the 'all' baseline, and one Verification invariant still protects src/main.py.
evidence: `grep -l 'from src' tests/test_*.py | wc -l` -> 39; `grep -l 'simorgh' tests/test_*.py | wc -l` -> 0; `grep -rl 'from src' simorgh/ simloader.py sim.sh` -> nothing.
src/: 16,441 lines; last commit touching src/ 2026-09-09, tests/test_*.py 2026-09-06.
simloader.py:551-552 `if all_tests or not paths: return ["tests"]`; .simorgh_loader/unit_baseline.json `{"tests": 5969}` vs core 3348.

simorgh/verification/config.py:28-31 `_DEFAULT_INVARIANTS = {"src/main.py": ["AuditGate(", ...], ...}`; simorgh/execution/ invariant `verifier.verify(` matches exactly 1 file of the package (grep -rl -> 1), so the prefix rule would fail any other execution/ file if it ever applied.
tests/test_e2e_cli.py:1-9 is the only process-boundary e2e in the repo and it spawns `python -m src.main`.
findings.why_it_matters: A quarter of the suite by test count and 13% by lines is maintenance weight that verifies nothing the running system does, inflates the 'suite larger than the code' number, and keeps `--all-tests` at ~20 minutes. The only genuine process-level e2e pattern in the repo lives in that dead tree instead of being ported.
findings.recommendation: Move src/ and tests/test_*.py to an archive branch or delete them (git keeps them), drop the src/main.py invariant, and port test_e2e_cli.py's pattern to v2 as a single CORE test that spawns `python -m simorgh --self-check` with a 60s timeout and asserts exit 0.

findings.title: No regression benchmark for the daily path (chat + voice)
findings.claim: Nothing measures turn latency, prompt size or trace-writer drops over time for the path the family actually uses; the benchmark unit measures model capability on public suites, not the system's own regressions.
evidence: `grep -rli 'latency|p95|p50|regression' tools simorgh/benchmark tests/simorgh/benchmark` -> tools/bench_recall.py (memory retrieve scaling), simorgh/benchmark/swebench.py, one benchmark test.
simorgh/voice/bench.py:12,89 measures one STT sample's latency_s; no writer stores it and `grep -rln 'voice/bench|voice bench' docs/findings docs/*.md` finds only EVOLUTION.md.
kernel/metrics.py:20-27: `MetricsHistoryWriter` snapshots per-subsystem gauges to metrics:history, but no test or tool reads that stream for a threshold or a delta.
memory note project_test_suite_speed.md records that the gate went 8m20s -> under a minute only after profiling by hand; nothing prevents the same drift returning.
tests/simorgh/voice: 45 files, the only time-shaped one is test_a_slow_engine_is_waited_for.py (a behaviour, not a budget).
findings.why_it_matters: The project's own history (STT degrading under self-inflicted load, provider silent failover, 8-minute gates) is a history of latency regressions discovered by the human noticing. With the offline floor provider already wired into conftest, a deterministic timing run is cheap and would have shown each of those as a number before a person felt it.
findings.recommendation: Add tools/daily_bench.py: boot a Kernel with the floor provider and a temp data_dir, push 20 scripted lines through Interface._handle_line and 5 fake voice transcripts, record per-turn wall time, assembled prompt bytes, bus queue depth and TraceWriter.failed/dropped, append one JSON line to results/daily_bench.jsonl, and have `bless` print the delta against the last blessed line (warn at +25%). No model call, under a minute.

findings.title: The suite is in-process and uses real time; the two incidents that bricked the system were process-level
findings.claim: 5,515 tests run entirely inside pytest's process with 153 real asyncio.sleep(>0) waits and no timeout plugin configured, while the incidents the project remembers (a non-compiling simloader, Ctrl-C ignored by a busy tool thread) live at the process boundary no v2 test crosses.
evidence: `grep -rhE 'asyncio.sleep\(0?\.[0-9]+|asyncio.sleep\([1-9]' tests/simorgh | wc -l` -> 153; `time.sleep(` -> 8; tests/simorgh/execution/media/test_cast.py with a fake backend: `32 passed in 32.41s` (measured).
`grep -rn '"-m", "simorgh"' tests/simorgh` -> nothing; sim.sh:35-52 exists because 'a syntax error in simloader.py bricked the system completely'.
No pytest.ini/pyproject/setup.cfg; `pip list` shows pytest-xdist 3.8.0 and pytest-asyncio 0.26.0 but no pytest-timeout; conftest.py registers only the `live` marker.
memory project_test_suite_speed.md: FakeClock.sleep busy-spins the scheduler in booted-Kernel tests (test_flow_5_pause_resume_stop ~17s), still open.
findings.why_it_matters: Real sleeps make the gate's 45 seconds drift upward silently and make xdist results order-sensitive; the absence of any subprocess test means the one file whose failure has no rollback (simloader.py) and the shutdown path are verified only by sim.sh's runtime guard.
findings.recommendation: Add pytest.ini with `timeout = 120` (install pytest-timeout) and `-p no:cacheprovider`, replace the FakeClock spin with a scheduler that awaits a clock event, and add one CORE subprocess test that runs `python simloader.py status` and `python -m simorgh --self-check` and asserts exit 0 within 60s.

findings.title: Knowledge about what works is spread across four records
findings.claim: docs/findings (5 dated files), docs/EVOLUTION.md (5,254 lines of history the notes say is stale), ~40 memory notes, and observer findings JSONL under ~/.cache all record measured results, so the next session has to reconcile them rather than read one.

tools/observer_kit.py:60-79: FINDINGS_ROOT = ~/.cache/simorgh-observer-findings, outside the repo; tools/aggregate_findings.py clusters them but writes nowhere in docs/.
Task brief for this review: 'docs/EVOLUTION.md (5,254 lines) is a HISTORY; a bug it describes has very likely been fixed since.'
findings.why_it_matters: The findings process is the right idea (dated, measured, cited) and it is only three days old; the risk is that it becomes a fifth place rather than the place, and that observer output evaporates in a cache directory.
findings.recommendation: Have aggregate_findings.py emit a docs/findings/<date>-observer-wave.md skeleton (clusters, files, lines) that the coordinator edits; freeze EVOLUTION.md with a header pointing at docs/findings; keep memory notes as pointers into findings rather than as parallel records.

result.reasoning: Every cited fact checks out against the code as it is today, and the claim is not in the known-findings list (the existing reviews praise the HMAC as "a stellar security pattern" / "architecturally sound" without stating its threat model). The token is exactly HMAC-SHA256 over action_id|tool|args_sha256|expiry (contracts/security.py:38-40) verified constant-time plus expiry (43-58) and replay-guarded (execution/verifier.py:35-55). The secret is scoped to guardian+execution via NEEDS_HMAC_SECRET (kernel/registry.py:50) and ContextFactory (kernel/context.py:119-121), but that scoping is a lookup discipline, not a process boundary: both services store the raw bytes on `self._secret` (guardian/service.py:165, execution/service.py:142) inside the same interpreter as every other subsystem. The live deployment is single-process: ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml has no [runtime] section, so mode defaults to "single" (kernel/api.py:34). The claim is actually slightly stronger than stated: even in local-multi, WorkerKernel hosts only Orchestration with hmac_secret=b"" (kernel/service.py:606-641), so Guardian and Execution co-reside in the kernel process in every mode and the approval token never crosses a process boundary; only the subsystem-identity tokens (IdentityRegistry, service.py:173) do. The dedupe map's own comment (guardian/service.py:139-157) confirms the mechanism's real catch was an at-least-once redelivery minting a second token that tripped the replay guard, i.e. an ordinary fault, not an adversary. Minor citation drift: the verifier logic is at verifier.py:35-55, not 43-57. The parts of the claim that lean on other findings (unverified inputs upstream, unconfined effects downstream) are cross-references I did not independently re-verify, but the core assertion about what the HMAC does and does not prove stands. Classification as (a) a correct-but-over-read mechanism at low severity is fair; the recommendation (keep it, state its threat model, work on confinement) follows.

result.corrected_claim: The approval token is HMAC-SHA256 over action_id|tool|args_sha256|expiry, minted by Guardian and re-verified (with a replay guard) by Execution, and the secret is allow-listed to those two subsystems. But Guardian and Execution live in the same Python process in every runtime mode -- the live config runs "single", and even "local-multi" only moves Orchestration into workers (kernel/service.py:630-636), keeping Guardian and Execution together with the raw secret on each service's `self._secret`. So the token proves that what Execution ran is the exact action Guardian approved and defends against bugs and redelivery (the one case it has demonstrably caught, guardian/service.py:139-157), not against in-process code; it says nothing about whether the approval was sound or the effect bounded.

label: refute:proportionality:Adaptive immunity never learns from shel

result.concern: Composition root, lifecycle, configuration, and the boot/rollback harness (simorgh/kernel/*, simloader.py, sim.sh, simorgh/__main__.py, ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml)
result.summary_of_what_is_actually_there: The composition root is simorgh/kernel/service.py::Kernel.boot (lines 157-327): it opens the Ledger (make_ledger, line 163), builds one bus backend and the Kernel's own BusClient with a ReservedTopologyPolicy (lines 173-186), records the effective config to a `config:effective` stream after configcheck.report (lines 202-214), then walks registry.LAYERS (registry.py:39-46, six layers: bus/ledger -> cognition/memory/worldmodel -> guardian/execution/verification/planning -> learning/reflection/curiosity -> persona/benchmark/voice/interface -> orchestration) through Supervisor.start_layer, which starts each layer concurrently under a hardcoded 30 s boot timeout and waits for every service's health() before the next layer (supervisor.py:51-79). registry.py is the only module that imports other subsystems' Service classes (verified: all 14 cross-subsystem import edges originate in kernel/); every Service is constructed with no arguments except guardian/execution, which receive a Config built by the Kernel (registry.py:145-146, service.py:217-218). ContextFactory.build (context.py:111-143) hands each subsystem its own BusClient bound to its source name, `config=self._config.section(name)`, a deny-by-default ScopedSecretStore (plus `__hmac__` for guardian/execution only), a per-subsystem data dir, and (in multi-process modes) a self-issued identity token. Config is loaded by kernel/config.py::load_config with search order --config > $SIMORGH_CONFIG > ./simorgh.toml > ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml (lines 38-51), and the live file has [voice], [interface], [execution], [cognition.providers.ollama] sections and no [runtime]/[bus]/[ledger] (so mode=single, bus=memory, ledger=jsonl). Fourteen services adopt their section in start() via `if self._config_from_caller is None and ctx.config: Config.from_mapping(...)`, guardian/execution via the Kernel constructor, and only bus.Service takes none, so the memory note that 12 subsystems ignore their config is stale: 16 of 17 consume it. After the layers, the Kernel starts the Scheduler (durable timers rebuilt from the `schedule` ledger stream, scheduler.py), a ProcessMetricsPublisher and MetricsHistoryWriter on metrics_every_s=10 s, subscribes to system.pause/resume/stop/restart, appends state transitions to the `system` stream before publishing system.state.changed (state.py, service.py:388-447), and restores a persisted autonomous pause (service.py:366-386). Shutdown (service.py:527-556) unsubscribes, stops the periodic tasks, appends `stopped`, then Supervisor.stop_all stops layers in reverse under one shared grace budget (supervisor.py:126-147); kernel/cli.py::_cmd_run wraps this in a Stopper whose first SIGINT/SIGTERM publishes system.stop and arms a grace+10 s watchdog, and every exit path ends in `_exit_now` -> os._exit after pkill -P and stty sane (cli.py:86-200). The concurrency model is one asyncio loop, 138 `asyncio.to_thread` sites for blocking work on the default executor, 46 blocking `subprocess.run` calls (mostly inside those threads), one daemon REPL thread bridged with `run_coroutine_threadsafe(...).result()` (interface/service.py:261, 720), and one ThreadPoolExecutor for dashboard feeds. sim.sh (cd to the repo root, exports SIMORGH_EXECUTION_REPO_ROOT, restores simloader.py from the newest sim-good tag if it will not compile, then execs `python simloader.py run`) launches simloader.py, a stdlib-only bootloader that, unless `.simorgh_loader/last_green.json` matches a clean HEAD, runs the core pytest selection (`-n auto`, ~3348 tests) with a skip key, judges the verdict from pytest's summary line plus a shrink baseline, tags green clean commits `sim-good-NNNN`, rolls back with `git checkout -q <tag>` on failure (refusing if the tree is dirty), relaunches Sim with a plain `subprocess.run`, re-gates on exit code 75 (the REPL `restart`), and treats any non-zero exit within 60 s as a bad image.
strengths: Composition-root discipline is real, not aspirational: a scripted import matrix over all 18 packages found exactly 14 subsystem-to-subsystem import edges and every one originates in simorgh/kernel/ (registry.py + configcheck.py + service.py); no subsystem imports another, and tests/simorgh/test_module_boundaries.py enforces it. The 'talks only via the bus' story holds at the import level.

Layered boot with the safety layer before any proposer: registry.py:39-46 puts guardian/execution in layer 3 and orchestration last; supervisor.py:51-79 starts a layer concurrently and refuses to proceed until every member's health() is ok/degraded, so no Worker exists before Guardian and Execution are up.

Per-subsystem Context is well shaped: context.py:111-143 gives each subsystem its own BusClient bound to its source name (so trace/metrics/policy see the real publisher), its own [section] dict, a per-subsystem data dir, and a deny-by-default ScopedSecretStore with prefix families (secrets.py:96-132) plus a curated DEFAULT_SECRETS map (registry.py:64-82) so features are not switched off by a forgotten config line.

Honesty instrumentation around config: configcheck.py probes each section by building the Config from the empty mapping and from the written one and warns when they are identical (lines 1-21, 262-284), corrects the inverted guardian default (EFFECTIVE_DEFAULTS, lines 31-45), and Kernel._record_effective_config writes value+source per field to a `config:effective` stream (service.py:466-525) that the `config` REPL command reads back.

The loader honours its one principle on the code side: simloader.py never imports simorgh (stdlib only), reads pytest's own summary line rather than trusting the exit byte, refuses 'no tests ran', refuses a run that shrank more than 10% against the last green baseline, and withholds a tag when untracked code would have been imported (unit_verdict lines 660-699; untracked_code 492-503; cmd_run 985-1000). sim.sh:41-55 restores a non-compiling loader from the newest sim-good tag, closing the 'Sim bricks its own bootloader' hole.

Shutdown is bounded end to end: one shared grace budget across all layers (supervisor.py:126-147), a watchdog that fires even for REPL-initiated stops (cli.py:191-192), the final `stopped` state appended before the ledger layer closes (service.py:538-549). The live `system` stream shows 244 stopping / 244 stopped over 255 boots, i.e. orderly shutdown completes essentially every time.

State is durable where it matters: transitions are appended to the ledger before system.state.changed is published (state.py docstring, service.py:388-397); a human's `auto off` survives restarts (service.py:366-386, state.py:56-67); schedules are a ledger projection rather than threading.Timer (scheduler.py:14-18, 89-118).

Boot cost is not the ledger's size: jsonl.py:203-244 trusts index.json entries whose byte size matches, and a measured scandir+stat over the live 118,215 stream files took 0.27 s with index.json parsing in 0.07 s; importing the whole composition root (build_factories, all 17 Service modules) takes 0.29 s. The 45 s boot is the test gate, not the system.

findings.title: The Supervisor never supervises: no health ticker, restart never restarts, auto-pause on Guardian-down is unreachable
findings.claim: Supervisor.poll_once (which is the only path to _restart, and therefore to _on_critical_down) has no production caller, health_every_s is parsed and never read, and _restart stops a service without ever calling start() again, so the S3 invariant 'Guardian/Execution down => system pauses' is not enforced at runtime and the status snapshot's per-subsystem health is frozen at boot-time values.
evidence: grep -rn 'poll_once\|_health_task' across simorgh/ and tests/: the only callers are tests/simorgh/kernel/test_supervisor.py:99,106,122 and tests/simorgh/integration/test_guardian_down_autopauses.py:76, whose docstring (lines 8-13) says: 'Phase 0 has no periodic health-poll driver wired into Kernel.boot() yet -- poll_once() is called directly here, standing in for that future ticker.'
simorgh/kernel/service.py:157-327 (Kernel.boot) creates the Supervisor at 226-230 and never create_task()s a poll loop; grep 'health_every_s' hits only kernel/config.py:81,115 and kernel/api.py:43.

simorgh/kernel/supervisor.py:116-124: after `await supervised.service.stop()` the method ends with the comment 'The concrete restart (re-start()) is driven by the caller (Kernel service loop)' -- no such loop exists; supervisor.py:79 stores `asyncio.current_task()` (the boot coroutine) as the service's task.
simorgh/kernel/metrics.py:101-102 `_on_health: pass  # the supervisor's own poll is the source of truth` and 110-119 snapshot() reads s.status/s.last_health, which only _boot_one and poll_once write.

docs/blueprint/subsystems/03-kernel.md:281-290 promises 'Health is polled every health_every_s; three consecutive non-ok polls -> degraded ... Guardian and Execution are special: if either is down, the Kernel transitions to paused automatically'.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the project's own dominant bug shape (designed slot, one side built, nobody drives it) sitting in the kernel that is supposed to catch it elsewhere. The safety story leans on 'nothing may execute without the safety path' being enforced by wiring; today it is hoped for. The dashboard's subsystem health column is a boot-time screenshot, and three [runtime] knobs (health_every_s, supervisor_backoff_s, supervisor_max_restarts_per_10m) are inert while being exempt from the dead-config probe (configcheck.KERNEL_SECTIONS).
findings.recommendation: Pick one of two small changes. (a) Wire the ticker: in Kernel.boot after the layer loop, `self._health_task = asyncio.create_task(self._health_loop())` that sleeps health_every_s, awaits supervisor.poll_once(), and publishes system.health for each changed service; cancel it in shutdown. (b) For one laptop, simpler and probably better: delete the in-process restart/backoff machinery and keep only 'down => pause + publish', because a subsystem that crashed mid-state is safer taken down with the process and relaunched by the loader, which is already the process-level restart mechanism. Either way, delete the dead runtime fields or make configcheck cover [runtime].

findings.title: A cwd-relative `simorgh.toml` write can silently shadow the real config on the next boot
findings.claim: interface/dispatch.py appends MCP approvals to `Path("simorgh.toml")` relative to the process cwd, which under sim.sh/simloader is the repo root where no simorgh.toml exists; the Kernel's search order prefers ./simorgh.toml over ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml, so after one `mcp approve` and the advertised restart the entire live configuration ([voice], [interface], [execution] secrets, [cognition]) is replaced by a file containing one MCP block, with no warning.
evidence: simorgh/interface/dispatch.py:79 `_SIMORGH_TOML_PATH = Path("simorgh.toml")`; :2167-2173 `with _SIMORGH_TOML_PATH.open("a", ...)` then `return Outcome(f"approved: wrote ... to {_SIMORGH_TOML_PATH} -- restart Sim to load it")`.
simorgh/kernel/config.py:44-50: `cwd_candidate = Path("simorgh.toml"); if cwd_candidate.is_file(): return cwd_candidate` before the data_dir candidate.

sim.sh:13 `cd "$REPO_ROOT"`; simloader.py:1057 `subprocess.run([..."-m", "simorgh", "run"...], cwd=repo, ...)`; `ls /Users/saeed/ws/Simorgh/simorgh.toml` -> 'No such file or directory'; the live config is ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml.

A second, independent config path exists: simorgh/contracts/settings.py:162-170 re-implements the search order 'without importing' the kernel (ignores --config and SIMORGH_RUNTIME_DATA_DIR) and :185 is a TOML writer; contracts/places.py:57-62 reads the TOML directly with a module-level `_cache`.
findings.why_it_matters: Configuration has one reader in the kernel but at least three independent locators/writers outside it. The failure is silent and total: configcheck cannot warn because the shadow file parses fine, and `config` will happily report the new path. It also means a `--config other.toml` run has tools persisting settings into a different file from the one being read.
findings.recommendation: Make the path a single fact: add `config_path` to Context (ContextFactory already holds LoadedConfig.path) and have every writer (settings.py, places.py, dispatch.py) use it; delete the cwd candidate from find_config_path (a daemon launched from a repo root should not read a repo-relative config); have contracts/settings.py call kernel.config.find_config_path instead of copying it.

findings.title: The loader boots and rolls back the development checkout, so rollback is refused when it is needed, detaches HEAD, and diverts Sim's own landings
findings.claim: Running the A/B-image pattern against the same git checkout the creator edits means rollback is disabled whenever the tree is dirty (most of the time during development), a successful rollback leaves HEAD detached with no roll-forward, worktree landing then fast-forwards that detached HEAD instead of main, and sim.sh's loader self-repair itself dirties the tree and thereby disables rollback.
evidence: simloader.py:877-897 cmd_rollback: `if is_dirty(repo): say("refusing: the working tree has uncommitted changes..."); return 2` (no write_note on this path), then `git checkout -q target` (line 888) -- detached HEAD; grep for 'checkout' in simloader.py finds no return-to-branch logic.

.simorgh_loader/decisions.jsonl lines 59-60: `{"kind": "watchdog", "commit": "a68ed8e", "why": "Sim exited 2 after 7s, inside the 60s watchdog"}` followed 23 s later by `{"kind": "gate_skipped", ...}` with no rollback/rollback_failed note between -- the watchdog rollback was silently refused.

simorgh/execution/worktree.py:192 `main_head = _git(self.repo, "rev-parse", "HEAD")` and the landing `merge --ff-only` (worktree.py, ~line 229) run in the live repo, i.e. 'main' means whatever HEAD is; the module docstring (lines 22-25) says 'fast-forward main'.
sim.sh:45 `git checkout "$LAST_GOOD" -- simloader.py` modifies a tracked file, which is_dirty (simloader.py:444-450, `--untracked-files=no`) then reports as dirty.

git log: all three real rollbacks (dd54876, 5cadca0, 424c478) were on commits authored 'Saeed'; `git log --author=Simorgh --oneline | wc -l` = 94 of 856 commits -- Sim's own commits land pre-gated via worktree.land and have never been the thing rolled back.
Memory note feedback_live_checkout_uncommitted: 'sim.sh boots from the repo I edit; half-done edits get gated and block rollback'.
findings.why_it_matters: The bootloader analogy works in embedded systems because the image slot is not the engineer's workbench. Here the same directory is the workbench, the deploy target, and Sim's landing target, so the three interfere: the human's uncommitted edit blocks the rollback, the rollback strands the human on a detached HEAD, and Sim's next patch lands on that detached HEAD where a later `git checkout main` orphans it.
findings.recommendation: Separate deploy from dev with one git worktree: the loader owns `~/.simorgh/live` (git worktree add on a `live` branch), boots Sim from it, and rollback/roll-forward are `git -C live reset --hard sim-good-NNNN` / `... main` there -- the dev tree's state never matters, HEAD is never detached in the creator's checkout, and landing targets the `main` branch by name (`rev-parse main`, `update-ref`), not HEAD. Roughly 50 lines in simloader.py and sim.sh. Also write a note on the dirty-refusal path so Sim can see that a rollback did not happen.

findings.title: The boot gate is skipped by hand about half the time, gates the wrong moment, and runs the judged code with the live environment
findings.claim: The 45-48 s core gate is bypassed with the skip key on 34 of 70 gate opportunities in the last five days, cannot be reused while any untracked .py exists (as now), duplicates the landing-time gate that already protects Sim's own commits, treats a config/boot error as a bad image, and inherits the operator's environment and $HOME so the loader's 'never runs the code it is judging' principle is violated on the environment side.
evidence: .simorgh_loader/decisions.jsonl (99 decisions, 2026-09-14..18): gate_skipped 34, blessed 20, gate_reused 7, tag_withheld 5, gate_failed 4, restart 24, rollback 3, watchdog 1; restart -> next gate decision median 45 s, p90 58 s.
.simorgh_loader/unit_baseline-core.json: {"tests": 3348, "seconds": 45.67}; a whole-suite gate in the notes: '5940 passed ... in 445.02s (0:07:25)'.

`python3 simloader.py status`: 'untracked CODE -- the gate would run it, no tag can be earned while it is here: simorgh/big.py' (a 2-line scratch file) -- source_fingerprint returns '' so already_verified never matches (simloader.py:916-954).

simloader.py:383-386 `subprocess.Popen(argv, cwd=cwd, ...)` with no env=; sim.sh:22 exports SIMORGH_EXECUTION_REPO_ROOT into that environment; tests/simorgh/kernel/test_the_suite_cannot_see_the_operators_env.py documents the consequence ('5,007 files written into the live data_dir') and the fix lives in the suite's own conftest, i.e. in the judged code.

simloader.py:1042-1048 treats any non-zero exit inside 60 s as a bad image; kernel/cli.py:392-397 returns 2 for both ConfigError and KernelBootError; the one real watchdog event was 'Sim exited 2 after 7s'.
simorgh/execution/worktree.py:22-25: landing already runs 'the gate -- the whole suite -- in a copy of the rebased tree; fast-forward main'.
findings.why_it_matters: A gate that the operator routinely skips protects the tag ledger, not the boot. Its real catches (4 gate_failed) were all the creator's own un-tested commits; Sim's commits are gated at landing. Meanwhile every restart pays 45 s or a keypress, and the gate cannot tell 'the code regressed' from 'the house is offline'.
findings.recommendation: Move the default to gate-at-change, not gate-at-boot: `run` reuses the last green verdict for the current commit regardless of untracked non-test scratch (or ignore untracked files outside tests/ and simorgh/ that the suite does not import), gates only when HEAD moved past the newest tag, and offers `--force-gate` for the rest. Give the pytest child a loader-side env allowlist (PATH, HOME=<tmp>, PYTHON*) so the judged code cannot inherit the live data dir. Split exit codes so a ConfigError (2) never triggers the watchdog rollback while a KernelBootError (3) does.

findings.title: Three deployment modes and a multi-process trust model carried by a single-process system, plus a self-check that proves stubs and is never called

findings.title: Under the loader, a terminal SIGINT SIGKILLs Sim 250 ms into its orderly shutdown
findings.claim: simloader.launch_sim uses a plain subprocess.run with no signal handling; a Ctrl-C reaches both processes, CPython's subprocess.run waits 0.25 s for the child and then kill()s it, so stop_grace_s, the Stopper watchdog, the final `stopped` ledger event and the loader's own bookkeeping are all skipped whenever the signal is delivered to the group.
evidence: simloader.py:1053-1057 `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "simorgh", "run", *sim_args], cwd=repo, env=env)`; grep 'KeyboardInterrupt|signal.' in simloader.py: no matches.

Standalone reproduction in the scratchpad (parent = plain subprocess.run, child = SIGINT handler doing a 3 s orderly shutdown, SIGINT sent to the process group): output 'parent: KeyboardInterrupt after 1.24 s' (1.0 s delay + 0.25 s _sigint_wait_secs), 'child alive 4s later: False', child.log 'got SIGINT' with no 'orderly shutdown DONE' line.
simorgh/kernel/cli.py:132-156 Stopper expects grace+10 s (stop_grace_s default 15, api.py:46).

Frequency is low in practice: ~/.simorgh/ledger/streams/system.jsonl stop reasons are repl_exit 158, user exit 52, repl_restart 31, signal 1; interface/tui.py:493 keeps ISIG off so Ctrl-C at the prompt is a keypress, not a signal. The path is live during boot, the gate, the readline fallback, headless runs, and `kill -INT -<pgid>`.
findings.why_it_matters: Two process supervisors (loader and Kernel Stopper) that do not know about each other: the Kernel's carefully bounded shutdown is unreachable in the standard launch path for the one signal a terminal sends. A SIGKILL mid-append is exactly what the ledger's fsync discipline exists to survive, but the `stopped` state, notes and tags are lost.
findings.recommendation: In launch_sim, ignore SIGINT in the loader for the child's lifetime (`signal.signal(SIGINT, SIG_IGN)` before Popen, restore after), or use Popen + wait() and on KeyboardInterrupt wait(timeout=stop_grace+15) before killing. Five lines.

findings.title: `simorgh status` boots a second full Kernel and reports on itself; `trace`/`migrate-v1` ignore the configured ledger backend

findings.title: os._exit is a symptom, not the disease: blocking work has no registry or cancellation, one REPL command blocks the event loop, and the boot timeout is a hardcoded constant
findings.claim: The concurrency model (one asyncio loop, default-executor threads for blocking calls, one daemon REPL thread bridged by run_coroutine_threadsafe) is coherent, but 138 to_thread sites and 46 blocking subprocess.run calls are untracked and uncancellable, so shutdown can only race a watchdog and hard-exit; `!<cmd>` runs subprocess.run on the loop thread; and Supervisor's 30 s per-service boot timeout is not configurable.
evidence: Counts (grep -rn --include='*.py' over simorgh/): asyncio.to_thread 138 (execution 19 files, voice 10, cognition 4, interface 3), threading.Thread( 1 (interface/service.py:261, daemon=True), run_coroutine_threadsafe 1 real site (interface/service.py:720), subprocess.run( 46, ThreadPoolExecutor 1 (interface/dashfeeds.py:925), asyncio.run( inside the package 1 (a generated skill-driver string, execution/tools.py:2721).
simorgh/kernel/cli.py:86-129 `_HARD_EXIT = os._exit` ... `_exit_now` (pkill -P, stty sane, os._exit) and :194-200 -- every exit path, including a clean one, ends in os._exit.

simorgh/interface/dispatch.py:166-172 `async def run_shell(...)`: `result = subprocess.run(command, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout)` with no to_thread -- the bus (voice, HTTP, Telegram) stalls for the command's duration. By contrast guardian/rules.py:507 correctly wraps run_bandit in asyncio.to_thread.
simorgh/kernel/supervisor.py:40 `boot_timeout_s: float = 30.0`; service.py:226-230 constructs Supervisor without passing it.
findings.why_it_matters: For one laptop the hard exit is an acceptable trade, but the Kernel cannot make any promise about in-flight tool work at shutdown, and the one loop-blocking call is on the path a human uses when things are already slow.
findings.recommendation: Wrap run_shell in asyncio.to_thread; expose boot_timeout_s in [runtime]; longer term, route long blocking tool work through subprocesses the Execution service tracks (pid list) so shutdown can terminate them deterministically instead of pkill -P at exit.

Only two rules read it: `ModeRule` (rules.py:257, plan mode and locked posture) and `ReversibilityRule` (rules.py:725-740, read_only -> allow, irreversible -> escalate). `grep -n "ctx.tool" simorgh/guardian/rules.py` hits only lines 257 and 298. `ProtectedRule` explicitly refuses to honour `read_only` for any proposal carrying a `code`/`command` argument (rules.py:116 `_CODE_ARG_KEYS = ("code","command")`, rules.py:286-300), and Denylist, Shellcheck, Scope, StaticAnalysis, Package, Grant, Immunity and Budget key on args, never on the label. So a `run_shell` relabelled read_only still gets the protected-path scan, denylist, shellcheck and scope checks; the relabel only buys (a) skipping the irreversible->human escalation and (b) passing in plan mode/locked posture. And (a) is already moot in the running system: kernel/service.py:188-200 sets `irreversible_requires_human=False` as sim.sh's baseline and ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml has no [guardian] override (`grep -n "guardian\|irreversible" ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml` returns nothing). Adding orchestration/ and profiles.py to the protected list would freeze the very layer the corrigibility design says must remain evolvable (guardian/config.py:17-20), which is disproportionate for one laptop and one developer. Subscribing Guardian to tool.registered is cheap but introduces a registration-ordering/replay dependency for something two rules use; a ~10-line test pinning every builtin row to the execution registry, plus a Guardian-side `classify_call` for `home_call`, closes the real gaps with less machinery.

The fix is inside home_call (refuse or re-propose when worst=="human" and the proposal was not escalated, or consult the registry at proposal time), not a new protocol axis across 105 tools. result.concern: Proportionality and coherence of the whole: is this the right architecture for one person, one laptop, one family, and for the stated goal of self-improvement?
result.summary_of_what_is_actually_there: simorgh/ is 86,996 lines in 18 subsystem packages plus contracts, each exposing one `Service` (simorgh/*/service.py; kernel/registry.py:40-46 boots them in six health-gated layers). Subsystems really do talk only over the bus: a grep of `from simorgh.X` across every package finds no subsystem importing another besides the bus/ledger client packages, and tests/simorgh/test_module_boundaries.py enforces it. The bus is in-process (`memory` backend; ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml has no [bus] or [ledger] section, so bus/config.py:30 `memory` and ledger/config.py:18 `jsonl` are in force, mode `single` per kernel/api.py:34), yet it ships three bus backends (memory/sqlite/aws) and four ledger backends (jsonl/sqlite/dynamodb/memory), a WorkerKernel for a `local-multi` mode, a schema-version translator registry with zero translators (contracts/compat.py), and a JSON-schema projection of all 174 message types "for a non-Python subsystem one day" (contracts/schemagen.py:8). Every effect goes through Guardian: guardian/service.py:171 is the only subscriber to action.proposed, execution/service.py re-verifies the HMAC token, and 26,737 `action:<id>` ledger streams show no bypass -- but 22,849 of them (85%) are the dashboard's Ring WebRTC `offer/keepalive/close` signalling (httpapi.py:476-487 -> `ring_live`), at 3.6 proposals/minute over 107 hours. The Ledger is a directory of one JSONL file per stream plus one idempotency index file per stream: 118,215 stream files and 90,755 idem files, 1.4 GB, of which 88,356 are bus trace streams less than two days old (bus/trace.py writes one stream per trace_id; retention is 2d, compaction runs). The self-improvement loop that actually works is `improve` -> TASK_CREATE -> Orchestration PATCH-profile session in a git worktree -> `worktree_land` (orchestration/session.py:790) -> simloader gate; Sim has authored 94 commits this way (git log --author=Simorgh: 96 files, +8,069/-512). The subsystems that are supposed to learn from that -- World Model change history, Curiosity growth events, Reflection, Planning -- all subscribe to `learn.self_patch.applied`, which is published only by learning/pipeline.py, which runs only on `learn.pipeline.run`, which nothing publishes (learning/service.py:98-116 documents this and reports itself degraded). The live Self Model (~/.simorgh/worldmodel/self/SELF.md, v42) therefore says "What I've changed about myself: (none recorded yet)" and "How well I do it: unknown 97% (2466)", because learning/outcomes.py:84-94 types every chat turn as `unknown` (2,466 of 2,714 rows in learn:outcomes.jsonl). The user-visible surface is large and growing by anecdote: 104 Tool classes, 98 registered under default config (58 effectful), CHAT profile binds 72 tools and VOICE_CHAT 58 (orchestration/profiles.py), 29 CLI commands with 35 verb branches in a 2,234-line dispatch.py, 28 HTTP routes, five house/PIM/knowledge/security/energy "domains" living inside simorgh/execution (10.5k lines). Tests are 90,203 lines (larger than the code), docs 26,150 Markdown lines (EVOLUTION.md 5,254; blueprint 9,095; plans 5,923), and 28.5% of the non-blank lines inside simorgh/ are docstrings or comments, most written as dated changelog entries quoting the creator.
strengths: Module boundaries are real, not aspirational: `for p in <15 packages>; grep -rhoE '^(from|import) simorgh\.[a-z_]+' simorgh/$p` finds only bus/ledger client imports outside each package's own name and contracts; tests/simorgh/test_module_boundaries.py:55-128 enforces it. This is the single decision that makes the codebase deletable in pieces -- keep it.

The action path is genuinely structural: contracts/topics.py:295-313 SUBSCRIBE_ONLY_BY/PUBLISH_ONLY_BY reserve action.proposed to guardian and action.approved to execution; guardian/service.py:171 is the sole subscriber; execution/service.py:139-143 refuses to start without the HMAC secret and re-verifies every approval. A 3,000-stream sample of action:<id> shows received/decided/verified on every one, 5 denied (3 denylist, 2 paused), no bypass.

Worktree landing plus the loader gate is the right shape for self-modification on a live checkout: orchestration/session.py:790-810 lands via `worktree_land` and returns `blocked` on failure; simloader.py:547-575 gates each boot on the core tests and rolls back. 94 Sim-authored commits landed without bricking the system -- that is measured proof the isolation design works.

The lesson about silent handler failure was actually institutionalised: bus/factory.py:24-56 `default_handler_error` prints unconditionally to stderr with the three dated incidents that justify it, and is wired by default in make_backend.

Honest health is a real pattern, not a slogan: learning/service.py:117-125 reports `degraded` with the exact reason its purpose is unreachable; ledger/service.py reports `down` when it cannot persist.

The two-assembler duplication called out in docs/blueprint/07 is fixed: orchestration/context.py:2-3,133 deliberately excludes persona.voice/self.summary, and cognition/assembler.py:54-60 is the single owner.

Boot-time config self-check exists (kernel/configcheck.py) and the strict audit confirms it: of 542 dataclass config fields only 10 are unread anywhere in simorgh/ (config_audit.py output: 'TOTAL fields 542 unread anywhere 10').

The infrastructure share is not the problem: substrate (bus 2,157 + ledger 2,764 + kernel 4,045 + contracts 6,443) is 17.7% of the code; user-facing packages (execution, voice, interface, cognition, orchestration, memory, benchmark) are 65.5%. The proportion is fine; the incoherence is that the 14.7% growth layer is wired to the wrong events.

The Self Model's change history, Curiosity's growth events, Reflection's self-patch counters and Planning's follow-ups are all built and tested, and all fed by a pipeline that was superseded by the worktree loop. The architecture's growth layer is a spec'd machine bolted next to the machine that runs.
findings.recommendation: Delete learning/pipeline.py and correlator.py (the superseded pipeline) and the `draft_candidate`-shaped topics with them. Have orchestration's `_land` (session.py:790) publish `learn.self_patch.applied` (or rename it `self.patch.landed`, owned by orchestration) with subject, commit sha and test counts on success and `...reverted` on a gate rollback (simloader already knows the rollback; worldmodel/service.py:133 `_ingest_loader_rollback` shows the seam). findings.title: Typed config is read stringly: 123 `getattr(config, "x", default)` sites, 20 with a fallback that contradicts the dataclass default
findings.claim: Execution and Voice read their own typed Config dataclasses via getattr with a second, hand-typed default; in 20 sites that default is the opposite of the dataclass's, so behaviour silently flips whenever a test or tool passes a partial config, and the pattern is exactly what lets a 'designed slot nobody reads' hide from kernel/configcheck.py.

simorgh/voice/config.py:192 `conversation_window_s: float = 180.0` vs voice/session.py getattr fallback 0.0; `unplaced_follows_conversation` True vs False
kernel/configcheck.py:55-80 KNOWN_DEAD_FIELDS is a hand-maintained list precisely because data-flow dead fields cannot be discovered from the parsed Config
findings.why_it_matters: The dataclass Config was the right design: one typed source of truth per subsystem. getattr-with-default turns it into a stringly-typed dict with two defaults, which is how the project's dominant bug shape (a wire with one end) reproduces at the config level and how tests can pass against behaviour production never has.
findings.recommendation: Add a boundary-style test that forbids `getattr(<config>, "..."` in simorgh/ (the 5 legitimate cases can be allow-listed), then replace the 123 sites with direct attribute reads. It is a mechanical afternoon and it retires a class of bug.

label: refute:proportionality:Cognition's 'no real provider' health ti

result.corrected_claim: The Claude Code CLI provider ships with no price and no spend cap by default, so the per-request `max_cost_usd` gate cannot refuse it (its estimate is 0.0 by design) and a budget-driven skip of the primary leaves no per-call trace on the ledger. However: (1) the "$99.32" is Claude Code's self-reported API-equivalent `total_cost_usd`, not money -- the provider deliberately strips API keys so calls bill the creator's subscription (~/.claude.json has an oauthAccount and no API key), so the real cost is 5-hour quota, which the existing `max_calls=500 / window 18,000 s` already meters in the right unit; (2) ~$79 of the $99 fell on 09-10/09-11 while Together sat at exactly its old 1,500-call cap -- the creator fixed that on 09-11 (6,000 calls / $2), and every CLI burst since has happened with Together at 200-650 calls and $0.14-0.42 in-window, i.e. failure/timeout-driven failover, which IS logged (`cognition.provider_failed`) and announced on screen with its reason; (3) `max_spend_usd` on `claude_code_cli` already works today via one TOML line because `status()` sums the CLI's reported cost. What remains is a config-default omission plus one missing log line, not a wrong design.
result.reasoning:
Mechanism verified line by line: config.py:94-97 gives claude_code_cli only max_calls/window/timeout; budget.py:86-95 documents that unpriced providers estimate to 0.0 "so this never blocks them"; router.py:151-166 uses that estimate for the per-request gate and skips a can_spend=false candidate with a bare `continue` (no log); claude_code.py:147-151 reports input/output tokens 0 and cost from the CLI's total_cost_usd. Ledger tallies match the finding exactly (1,034 CLI events / $99.32; 6,991 Together / $4.56; purposes draft 526, review 287, chat 214, consolidate 7). Per-purpose CLI averages: chat $0.105 (206/214 over the $0.05 cap), draft $0.118, review $0.049.

Where the finding overreaches: (a) Cost framing. claude_code.py:20-21 and 51/161-165 strip ANTHROPIC_API_KEY/AUTH_TOKEN/OAUTH_TOKEN precisely so the call "bills the subscription, not a stray key"; ~/.claude.json shows an oauthAccount and no primaryApiKey. So $99.32 is quota-equivalent, not spend; the per-request dollar gate is the wrong instrument for a flat-rate backend, while calls-per-5h is the unit Claude's subscription actually meters. (b) Causal story. Bucketing CLI budget events by local hour against Together's rolling 24h window: 09-10 06-18h and 09-11 20-21h bursts (~$79) occurred with Together at exactly 1,500 calls (the old cap) -- budget-driven. config.py:76-84 records the fix (6,000 / $2). Every later burst (09-13, 09-15, 09-16 17-18h = 96 calls/$12.89) ran with Together at 205-635 calls and $0.14-0.42, and in the 09-16 hour Together simultaneously answered 74 chat + 50 draft + 55 review -- so those were slice-timeout/transient failovers, logged by router.py:227-230 and noticed by service.py:508-537, which names the cap when it is the reason (lines 521-531). Post-fix, budget-driven promotion has not recurred. (c) "no spend cap" is a default, not a capability gap: budget.py:64-68 sums payload cost_usd and 80-81 prefers the CLI's reported cost, so `max_spend_usd` under [cognition.providers.claude_code_cli] would bind today with zero code. ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml sets nothing for the CLI.

Proportionality at this scale: the useful parts of the recommendation (`only_purposes`, `max_spend_usd`, one `provider_skipped_budget` log line at router.py:165) are three TOML lines and one logger call -- cheap and worth doing. The parts that go too far: adding nominal price_in/out to drive the per-request dollar gate on a subscription backend, and dropping the CLI from the default order, which would remove the only working failover (gemini has 2 calls total in the ledger, ollama is appended behind the CLI at service.py:197-201 and is chat-only). Kind is closer to "right design, default under-configured" than "wrong-design"; severity high -> medium.
evidence: simorgh/cognition/config.py:94-97 -- `"claude_code_cli": ProviderConfig(max_calls=int(os.environ.get("SIMORGH_CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CALLS", "500")), window_seconds=18_000.0, timeout_seconds=180.0)` -- no price, no max_spend_usd (confirmed)
simorgh/cognition/config.py:76-84 -- comment recording the 2026-09-11 incident and the fix: Together max_calls 1500 -> 6000, max_spend_usd $2.0

result.reasoning:
Every element of the claim checks out against the code. Curiosity's `_on_provider_status` (simorgh/curiosity/service.py:231-238) reads only `budget.remaining_fraction` and `budget.free`. The single grep hit for `remaining_fraction` across simorgh/ and tests/ is that reader line; no publisher ever writes it. Cognition's two publishers of `cognition.provider.status` send `{window_seconds, calls, max_calls, spend_usd, max_spend_usd, exhausted}` on the 30s tick (cognition/service.py:452-460) and a bare `"budget": {}` on the provider-changed path (cognition/service.py:501-505). The contract (contracts/messages/cognition.py:61-72) types `budget` as an untyped `Obj()`, so no schema check could catch the mismatch. Nothing anywhere publishes `free` inside a budget object (the only `"free"` hits are verification cost tiers and a voice capability line). Consequently `worst_remaining` is never set, `_exploration_rate` (service.py:480-488) returns 1.0 unconditionally, and `budget_backoff_below_remaining`/`budget_stop_below_remaining` (curiosity/config.py:42-43) are dead. The curiosity test file has zero references to `_on_provider_status`, `worst_remaining`, or `any_free`, so the suite cannot notice. Guardian's `_fraction_used` (guardian/service.py:665-677) derives pressure from the real fields, confirming the reader's point that the correct derivation already exists next door. The blueprint (docs/blueprint/subsystems/13-curiosity.md:228-232, 278) specified `remaining_fraction`/`free` while 04-cognition.md:68 specified the fields actually sent: two blueprint pages disagree and the code implemented each side of its own page. Classification: (c) a genuine bug in the project's "unconnected wire" shape, not an architectural error.

Skeptic lens on proportionality: it is not an architectural problem, and the recommendation is not disproportionate; the fix is roughly five lines (derive `remaining` from calls/max_calls and spend/max_spend, tolerate the empty `{}` payload, honour `exhausted`, drop `free`). Compensating controls do exist and bound the damage: Cognition's own per-provider cap still refuses/fails over when `exhausted` (the router's floor path), the `min_explore_interval_seconds` cooldown (service.py:416-418) is real and tested, and the default caps are small (max_spend_usd $2/day, cognition/config.py:84/101). So the throttle's absence means curiosity spends the last 20% of a window at full rate rather than half, then hits the hard cap, rather than unbounded spend. That argues against raising severity, but not below medium: a designed safety throttle in the one subsystem that spends money on its own initiative silently never fires, has config keys that look live, and has no test. Curiosity also ignores Guardian posture entirely (no `posture` reference in curiosity/service.py), so Guardian's 90% budget-pressure tighten (guardian/config.py:102) does not reach it either; the Curiosity-side backoff was the only designed proportional brake.

result.reasoning:
The facts cited all check out: the default embedder is the 256-bucket sha256 hashing trick (simorgh/memory/embed.py:14-32), `embedder: str = "hashing"` (simorgh/memory/config.py:64), ~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml has no `[memory]` section (grep shows only [voice]/[interface]/[execution]/[cognition*]), the 0.000 paraphrase measurement is in embedders.py:6-14, `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_S = 0.25` is at orchestration/context.py:21, and docs/module-map.md:171-173 gives stt 1.8-6.8 s / llm 1.3-9.5 s. `sentence_transformers` is importable on this machine (find_spec -> True), so the switch from `auto` to `hashing` was a real decision, not a fallback.

The CAUSAL claim is where the finding goes wrong. (1) The 0.25 s timeout does not force hashing: the warm local cost is 47 ms, five times inside the budget, and the three recalls per turn are gathered concurrently so they share one timeout (context.py:233-262). Raising the timeout to 1 s changes nothing on the warm path and does not cover the 24.9 s cold path either. (2) The cold cost is already moved to boot: memory/service.py:68-75 spawns `warm()` as a background task and a recall arriving first waits on the same work (store.py:175-187). (3) The deciding reason recorded in commit 664d811 ("Recall stays on the hashing embedder") and config.py:51-63 is a QUALITY measurement, not latency: on the creator's own 2,422-record store, MiniLM-L6 moved the 0.000 paraphrase pairs only to 0.197/0.329 while "turn the lights on" vs "turn the lights off" rose 0.750 -> 0.893 and stayed the top score. Recall is pure top-k with no similarity threshold (store.py:238-258, no threshold in memory/*.py), so a 0.2 score is findable but easily outranked. The finding's recommendation to "raise the timeout and opt in local" ignores that the creator tried exactly this and measured that it did not fix the case it was chosen for. The actual mitigation the code chose for the cross-turn problem is the recency recall (`_MEMORY_RECENT_K = 6`, context.py:34-71) and the per-speaker recall, which address the falcon/sparrow and birthday cases without any embedder change.

The claim is exactly what the code does. simorgh/cognition/service.py:374 assigns `self._no_real_provider_since = self._ctx.clock.now() if floor else None` after every routed reply, so the timestamp is overwritten with `now` on each floor reply rather than pinned at the first one. health() at :242-247 then reports degraded only when `now - _no_real_provider_since > 300`, i.e. only after at least five minutes with NO further floor reply (and no real reply, which would reset it to None). While the system is actively answering from the floor every few minutes, health stays ok; it flips to degraded only once traffic stops. That is inverted relative to its evident intent ("no real provider available for Ns"). It is a genuine bug (category c), not a design choice, and the one-line fix the finding proposes is proportionate.

Skeptic lens on impact at this scale: the practical consequence is smaller than the finding's "the one health signal the whole system depends on" framing. result.reasoning: The core of the finding is true of the code today. simorgh/orchestration/scaffolds.py:638 returns "Right now it is {weekday} {date}, {HH:MM}." and :690-692 prefixes it to the task_rules body ahead of the task text and the whole per-tool notes table (the comment says 'Ahead of everything, including the task'); simorgh/orchestration/session.py:1243-1250 renders that with now=_epoch(self._clock) on every THINK; simorgh/cognition/assembler.py:52-68 re-requests PERSONA_VOICE, SELF_SUMMARY and (for chat) the user profile on every assemble(), and assemble() is called per THINK from cognition/service.py:290; service.py:296-333 joins every protected block (constitution, voice, self_summary, user_profile, task_rules, budget_hint/final_turn_hint) into a single role:system message; a repo-wide grep for cache_control|prompt_cach|cache_read|cache_creation|ephemeral finds nothing except together.py reading cached_tokens back from responses. Rendering the real profiles confirms the stamp is at char 0 of task_rules for chat, patch and voice, with ~5.5k-13k chars (~1.4k-3.2k tokens before the tool_instruction_block and skills catalog) following it. So a minute-granularity string sits ahead of the bulk of the prefix and defeats any prefix cache. Three parts of the claim are inaccurate or overstated: (1) the title's 'first line of the system prompt' is wrong -- constitution (~31 tokens), voice, self_summary and user_profile precede task_rules in the system message; the stamp is the first line of the task_rules block, so a few hundred tokens ahead of it are in principle cacheable while the thousands after it are not. (2) 'the budget hint changes every step' is only true inside the winding-down window (assembler.py:81 `steps_left <= _WINDING_DOWN_STEPS`); otherwise no budget block is emitted. (3) The recommendation 'cache_control on the static system block for Anthropic' has no target: simorgh/cognition/providers/ contains only claude_code.py (spawns the `claude` CLI per call with --system-prompt, :92-96), gemini.py, ollama.py and together.py -- there is no Anthropic Messages API client, so Simorgh cannot set cache_control; the actionable fix is stabilising the prefix (which is entirely under Simorgh's control) and, if desired, Gemini context caching. The finding is not in the known list (nothing there concerns prompt ordering or caching). On severity: the design defect is genuine and cheap to fix, but at this system's scale (one laptop, one family, ~1.4k-6k tokens per step, Together pricing in cents per million) the dollar and prefill-latency impact per session is modest, so 'high' overstates it; medium fits.
result.corrected_claim: The per-minute timestamp is the first line of the protected task_rules block (not of the whole system message; constitution, persona voice, self summary and user profile precede it), and that block plus the tool notes that follow it -- the bulk of the ~1.4k-6k-token system prompt -- is regenerated on every THINK, with persona voice / self summary / user profile re-requested over the bus each call. No provider in simorgh/cognition/providers/ sends a cache directive, and there is no Anthropic API provider to send cache_control through (the Claude route is a fresh `claude` CLI subprocess per call with --system-prompt); the budget hint appears only in the winding-down window, not every step. The fix is to order the system prompt static-to-dynamic, move the clock to day granularity in the system block and the minute into the user turn, and fetch persona/self/user-profile once per session, so that Together's server-side prefix caching (and the CLI's own) can hit.

Every number in the claim checks out against the code and the live config: CHAT offers 72 tools, max_steps=20, max_output_tokens=16_000, verify=False, no worktree (WORKTREE_KINDS = {patch, skill}), no resume (the scaffold itself says so), a 420s synchronous wait, a 12k-token chat input budget with no toml override, and the Ollama chat fallback at num_ctx=8192. I reproduced the prompt measurement exactly (task_rules ~3,247 tok + tool notes ~2,523 tok = ~5,771 tok; PATCH's rules are ~1,393 tok for comparison). The primary model has a 1M context per the project's own design doc, so the 12k budget is an unexamined Phase-1A default, not a fit to anything.

However, three things pull it down from a clean 'confirmed' at 'high'. (1) Two of its six legs are already reported in docs/architecture-third-opinion-2026-09-18.md: the 72-tool chat surface (lines 22, 160, 212, 222) and the 420s REPL block (line 144). (2) The 'already being snipped by compaction' consequence is arithmetic, not observed: the newest 40 trace streams contain zero context_too_large and one compaction event, and system.jsonl has none. (3) The mechanism is slightly wrong: cognition/service.py:334-338 appends tool_instructions OUTSIDE the budget check ('not counted ... a short fixed-shape string'), so the elastic room is ~12k minus task_rules minus constitution/voice/self_summary/user_profile, not 12k minus 5.8k; the uncounted ~2.5k tool-notes block is a small genuine bug (its comment is false for CHAT) and it makes the Ollama 8192 overflow worse, not better.

On the skeptic lens: the 20-step/16k numbers are not accidental, they are each a fix for a live-caught failure (12 steps failed 'build me a game' three times; 2,000 output tokens shredded a 147-line file to 54). The recommendation's 6-8 steps and 2-4k output would reinstate both failures unless start_task becomes the reliable build path first, so as written it is disproportionate for one developer. But the core design point survives and is materially strengthened by one thing the finding did not cite: because chat has no worktree, tool_root() (execution/tools.py:120-123) resolves a chat turn's apply_source_patch to config.repo_root, i.e. the LIVE checkout that sim.sh boots from, guarded only by ProtectedRule's prefix list. That is a design that is right (worktree isolation exists) undermined by the profile.

Net: wrong-design with a partly already-known surface and an overreaching recommendation; the cheap, high-value fixes are the input budget (12k vs 1M) and the uncounted tool-notes block, plus routing source edits out of chat.

(2) Broadcast delivery continuing during pause is likewise the specified behaviour (01-bus.md:447 "Command dequeue for non-system.* halts; events continue"), not a gap. (3) "Silently loses the event" is false: client.py:223 increments a `dropped` counter and logs `bus.handler_error`, and factory.py's default_handler_error prints the traceback to stderr unconditionally. What survives: backpressure and pause genuinely measure only group lanes (router.py:69, client.py:196-197), broadcast heaps are pushed unconditionally (memory.py:171) and their depth is not in the gauges; Ledger.tail exists (ledger/client.py:199) with zero callers, so "the ledger has them" means persisted, not re-delivered; and bus health (service.py:53-63) checks `dead` but ignores `dropped`. The count is also off: 161 subscribe sites, 7 with group= (finding missed orchestration/worker.py:214 group="workers" and kernel/metrics.py:91 group="kernel-status"; live gauges show 6 groups). The broadcast subscribers are projection/observer updaters (TASK_COMPLETED, TURN_COMPLETED, SYSTEM_STATE_CHANGED, DASH_STATE, TV_STATE); a dropped one yields a stale view, not a lost decision. The alternative recommendation to shrink the backend is disproportionate: the group machinery is not dead code, it carries the entire command path. And the live ledger shows the asymmetry has never bitten: 206,877 published, 656,420 delivered, 656,420 acked, no dropped/nacked/dead counters ever incremented, all queue depths 0. The "idem sidecar" cost is a ledger-side feature unrelated to bus broadcast; the finding conflates them. What remains actionable is small: add `dropped` (and broadcast heap depth) to bus health/gauges, and reword the code comment so "the ledger has them" is not read as a replay promise.

Where the finding overreaches is severity and the "why it matters". (1) The disk pressure is not the ledger's doing: the volume is 460 GB with 39 GB free; the whole ledger is 1.4 GB, 0.3% of capacity. Deleting it entirely moves free space from 8.4% to 8.7%. The march toward the 5% degraded line is caused by the other ~393 GB, not this design. (2) Growth is bounded, not runaway: `DEFAULT_RETENTION {"trace:": "2d"}` (compaction.py:36) makes 1.4 GB a steady state, and the last pass deleted 4,476 of 106,918 streams. (3) Compaction cost on the loop is small at this scale: per-id streams use `last_ts` from the in-memory index (jsonl.py:787-790, O(1)) and `delete_stream` is at most four unlinks (jsonl.py:691-694); ~4.5k unlinks every six hours is well under a second of blocking. The recommendation is disproportionate for the actual cost. Both (a) hourly trace streams and (b) a backend migration are real work and (a) breaks `trace <id>` (kernel/cli.py:249 reads `trace:{trace_id}`) unless an index is added. Two one-line fixes remove most of the waste with no migration: drop `idempotency_key` from trace events in trace.py:107 (eliminates 88k files / ~370 MB, and nothing is lost because trace dedupe never fires) and add the six uncaused broadcast types to `trace_sample` while deleting `_inbox.#` (config.py:60-64).
